P2400.d: P2400 is stored when the engine computer finds the drive line of the evaporative leak detection pump open, so the pump cannot be switched for the tank leak test. GM's tables for the sealed fuel system of the Volt (2011, 2016) compare the commanded and actual driver state and treat a low voltage in the off state, equal to more than 200 kOhm to ground, as an open; 20 failed samples out of 25 at 250 ms each set a Type B
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
No noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Corroded or loose pump connector, broken wire in the drive line
Open winding or internal fault in the leak detection pump
Coolant in the pump's vacuum supply line from a failed coolant pump changeover valve (VW Touareg 3.6)
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2401.d: P2401 means the control line of the leak detection pump is pulled to ground level, usually by chafed insulation touching the body or by an internal pump fault. GM's 2016 Volt table checks the low-side driver while it is switched off; a near-zero impedance of about 0.5 Ohm to controller ground counts as a short, and 20 of 25 samples of 250 ms set a Type B code over two trips.
s: Check engine light
Leak test not completed, EVAP readiness missing
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground near the tank or rear wheel arch
Internal short inside the leak detection pump
Water ingress in the pump connector causing a leakage path to ground

P2402.d: P2402 points to the opposite fault of P2401: the pump control line sits at supply voltage or the pump draws too much current. GM's Volt tables call it a short to power detected while the driver is on; when it is active the ECM runs an intrusive check, running the pump for 15 s on command, with a Type B code after 20 failed samples out of 25.
s: Check engine light that may persist after repair until software is updated
EVAP readiness incomplete, inspection may fail
c: Leak detection pump motor seized or drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Control module software that does not clear the fault after repair (Acura TLX Type S recall)

P2403.d: The sense circuit carries the feedback by which the engine computer knows what the leak detection pump is actually doing. P2403 is logged when that feedback is missing as if the line were open.
s: Check engine light
EVAP monitor not completed
More often after winter driving or car washes
c: Broken feedback wire or backed-out terminal at the pump connector
Water or ice trapped in the pump or its filter (Jaguar XJ)
Failed feedback element inside the pump

P2404.d: P2404 is a plausibility code: the pump feedback is electrically present but does not behave as the leak test expects. VW's 2014 Golf data book sets it when the sense signal stays high for more than 30.4 s (12 s on another engine) over 30 checks, or when high signal time during pumping adds up to more than 10 s.
s: Check engine light, often returning after clearing
EVAP readiness not set
c: Condensation inside the leak check module (Subaru ELCM, software update available)
Worn or sticking pump that no longer reaches its expected state in time
Coolant or debris in the pump's vacuum or vent line

P2405.d: P2405 is set when the feedback signal of the leak detection pump stays below its permitted window, typically from a short to ground on the sense line or a fault inside the pump. No public source states a voltage threshold for this code.
s: Check engine light, possibly set while the car is parked
No effect on drivability
c: Internal DMTL pump fault, often after dirt ingress through the dust filter
Corroded connector at the pump mounted near the rear wheel arch

P2406.d: P2406 is the mirror image of P2405: the pump feedback reads above its allowed range, as with a short to a voltage source or a sense line that floats high. Thresholds are not published.
s: Check engine light
Fault often appears after wet or freezing weather
c: Water or ice from road spray in the pump filter (Jaguar XJ)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage feed or open ground at the pump
Pump damaged by contamination entering through the dust filter

P2407.d: P2407 reports a pump feedback that jumps around instead of staying steady. On current-measuring DMTL pumps VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books define it precisely: the pump current fluctuates by more than 1 mA during the reference measurement, or it drops by more than 6 mA for at least 3 s while pumping, checked with the engine off and on.
s: Check engine light, sometimes only after the car has been parked
Code returns irregularly after clearing
c: Over-sensitive diagnostic calibration, fixed by ECM software update (Audi, VW 2022-23)
Loose contact or corrosion at the pump connector
Worn pump motor with unstable current draw

P2408.d: P2408 is the general circuit code for a sensor or switch that tells the engine computer whether the fuel cap or filler is closed. It is set when that circuit shows a fault not narrowed down to low, high, plausibility or dropout, which are P2410, P2411, P2409 and P2412.
s: Check engine light or fuel cap warning
EVAP leak test may be skipped
c: Faulty fuel cap or filler switch
Damaged wiring or connector at the filler neck
Aftermarket cap that does not actuate the switch correctly

P2409.d: P2409 is the plausibility code of the fuel cap sensor family: the circuit is electrically sound, but the reported cap state does not fit other information. A switch that never changes over a refuelling event, or one that reports closed while the leak test sees a gross leak, would be typical cases.
s: Check engine light or fuel cap message although the cap is tight
EVAP test results may be rejected
c: Cap switch mechanically stuck in one position
Wrong or damaged cap that does not operate the sensor
Misaligned filler door or neck after body repair

P240A.d: Some leak detection pump modules, such as the DMTL units on VW, Jaguar Land Rover and Maserati petrol engines, carry a small heating element that keeps moisture and ice from upsetting the pump and its pressure measurement. P240A is set when the heater's drive circuit appears open.
s: Check engine light
Further EVAP pump codes in cold or wet conditions
c: Burnt-out heating element inside the pump module
Broken heater wire or corroded terminal at the module connector
Missing supply voltage to the heater (fuse, relay)

P240B.d: P240B covers a heater control line of the leak detection pump that is held at too low a voltage, which in practice means a short to ground on the wire or inside the module. Per VW's 2014 data books for the Golf and Touareg, the code appears when the heater signal falls below roughly 2.74-3.26 V.
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not completed
c: Heater wire shorted to ground near the pump
Internal fault in the DMTL pump module (Land Rover replaces the pump)
Moisture in the connector creating a path to ground

P240C.d: P240C flags the heater circuit of the leak detection pump at the high end: VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books set it when the heater current exceeds about 2.2-4 A, which points to a shorted element or a line touching battery voltage. Jaguar's JTB00436 for the XJ (X351) quotes both P240C-00 and P240C-85, the 85 suffix marking a signal above range, among faults from water or ice in the DMTL filter; Land Rover's SSM69118
s: Check engine light
Other DMTL codes after frost or heavy rain
c: Shorted heating element in the pump module, often after water ingress
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty heater output stage in the engine control module

P240D.d: P240D applies only to vehicles running on a gaseous alternative fuel such as CNG or LPG, which CARB counts as alternate-fueled. It indicates a leak in the low-pressure part of the gas system, downstream of the pressure regulator.
s: Check engine light, gas mode may be disabled
Gas smell in the engine bay
Higher gas consumption
c: Leaking fitting or hose on the regulated low-pressure side
Leaking seal at the low-pressure filter or oil separator housing
Gas rail or gas injector seal leaking

P240E.d: P240E concerns the high-pressure side of a gaseous alternative-fuel system, from the storage cylinder through the tank valve and high-pressure line and filter up to the regulator. Pressures there are far higher than in the rail: CNG is stored at about 200-250 bar, and GM's PI1330 rates the 2015 Impala bi-fuel tank at 3,600 psi, with a high-pressure cut-off solenoid at the tank and a coalescing filter that is drained
s: Check engine light, vehicle switches to petrol or will not run on gas
Gas gauge falls while parked
Hissing noise or gas smell near the tank
c: Leaking high-pressure fitting or line between cylinder and regulator
Leaking tank valve or high-pressure cut-off solenoid
Leaking fill receptacle or its check valve
Leak at the high-pressure inlet of the regulator

P240F.d: P240F means the EGR system takes too long to follow a changed flow target. CARB has required diesel OBD to catch such slow response since model year 2010.
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or smoke during load changes
Engine power derate on heavy trucks
c: Faulty position sensor in the EGR valve (e.g. Hyundai solder-flux contamination)
Intermittent fault in the engine harness (Volvo/Mack D11/D13)

P2410.d: P2410 reports that the fuel cap sensor or switch circuit is held below its expected voltage window. Depending on how the switch is wired, this can mean a signal wire shorted to ground, a switch that is permanently closed to ground, or a sensor with a failed supply.
s: Check engine light
Fuel cap warning stays on or never appears
c: Signal wire shorted to ground at the filler neck
Missing supply voltage to the sensor

P2411.d: P2411 is stored when the fuel cap sensor or switch circuit reads above its normal window. With a pulled-up signal line this is what an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to the battery feed looks like, so it is often the code that follows a bodywork job or a filler-neck replacement.
s: Check engine light
Cap warning behaves as if the cap were permanently open
c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector, e.g. after body or filler-neck work
Signal wire shorted to battery voltage

P2412.d: P2412 covers a fuel cap sensor or switch whose signal drops out or flickers rather than holding one state, for instance from a loose terminal, a cracked wire that flexes each time the filler door is opened, or a worn switch contact. Brief interruptions of this kind can make the cap look open for a moment and spoil an EVAP test.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Occasional fuel cap warning with the cap closed
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Wire cracked where it flexes at the filler door

P2413.d: P2413 is a broad EGR performance code, and makers fill it in different ways. GM's 2011 6.6 L LGH Duramax uses it for insufficient flow: the air-mass controller deviation must pass a map value of 1.8 to 2.4 g per revolution for 10 s under steady fuelling, rated Type B.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or derate on diesels
Knocking or pinging under load on petrol engines
Failed emissions inspection
c: Soot or carbon restricting the EGR valve or passages
EGR valve not reaching commanded lift (actuator or position sensor)
Air-mass or pressure sensor error distorting the flow calculation

P2414.d: P2414 means the front air-fuel ratio sensor of bank 1 reports a reading that cannot come from real exhaust, usually a lean value caused by air leaking in ahead of the sensor or a sensor that is damaged. VW's January 2014 Golf/GTI data book uses two windows, a signal voltage of 3.10-4.81 V and a sensor signal of 2.5-3.2 V, with a second set near 2.5 V; another engine uses 3.1-4.77 V and 2.5-3.06 V.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption or uneven idle
Ticking noise from an exhaust leak
c: Air drawn in through a leak ahead of the sensor (manifold, gasket, cracked pipe)
Front sensor damaged by the catalyst-heating strategy (VW Jetta/Beetle 2.0, software update)
Loose, aged or contaminated air-fuel sensor

P2415.d: P2415 indicates that the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is not reading a representative exhaust sample - typically because outside air is drawn in through a leak near the sensor or the sensor is not seated correctly, so the reading is implausibly lean. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg evaluate the sensor signal voltage against two bands, 3.70-4.81 V and a lower band of 2.51-3.00 V or 3
s: Check engine light
Ticking exhaust noise when a leak is present
Higher fuel consumption or uneven running
c: Exhaust leak ahead of or near the sensor (manifold, gasket, flex pipe)

P2416.d: P2416 means the engine computer concludes that the two downstream oxygen sensors of bank 1 - sensor 2 after the first catalyst and sensor 3 after a second catalyst, as used mainly on SULEV/PZEV vehicles - are connected the wrong way round. No manufacturer publicly documents the detection logic for P2416.
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor not completing or giving implausible results
Usually no noticeable driveability change
c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair

P2417.d: P2417 is set when the engine computer finds that the two downstream oxygen sensors on bank 2 - sensor 2 behind the first catalyst and sensor 3 behind a second one - respond as if their wiring were exchanged. Such three-sensor layouts are typical of V-engines built to SULEV/PZEV limits.
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
Usually no noticeable driveability change
c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair

P2418.d: P2418 is the electrical check of the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve - an extra valve in the evaporative system whose job depends on the design. Ford calls it EVAP switching valve or vapor blocking valve; its 2012 and 2020-2023 OBD summaries check the driver continuously and set P2418 when a short, open or intermittent fault persists for more than 5 s, so at Ford this one code covers all circuit faults.
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
Possible fuel vapour odour or slow refuelling
c: Broken control wire or unplugged valve connector
Open solenoid coil in the switching valve
Corroded connector near the tank (road salt, splash water)

P2419.d: P2419 reports that the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads low - usually the control line is shorted to ground, or the driver stage measures too little voltage. Karma's Revero/GS-6 bulletin lists P2419 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve controlled by the ECM.
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
Often stored together with leak detection pump codes
c: Control wire shorted to ground (chafed near tank or frame)
Shorted coil in the switching valve or leak check module
Water ingress into the leak check module

P241A.d: With P241A the engine controller has concluded that the oxygen readings of the sensor ahead of the bank 1 catalyst and of the sensor behind it fit the opposite mounting positions, so the two plugs or harness legs are most likely crossed. FCA uses the code on the 2011 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7L Cummins diesel and calls it an oxygen concentration mismatch between sensors 1/1 and 1/2; bulletin 18-012-12 Rev.
s: Check engine light after work on the exhaust or the oxygen sensors
Mixture adaptation drifts, fuel trims look implausible
Catalyst or sensor codes set as follow-up faults
c: Upstream and downstream sensor plugs connected the wrong way round after a repair
Sensor harness rerouted or wrong replacement harness fitted
Detection software needing an update (FCA 6.7L Cummins)

P241B.d: P241B concerns only engines with a second exhaust bank, typically V engines: the controller has decided that the front and rear oxygen sensors of bank 2 deliver signals that belong to each other's position. No manufacturer bulletin names P241B publicly; the only published use of this check found is FCA's bank 1 version P241A on the inline-six Cummins, where it is described as an oxygen concentration mismatch.
s: Check engine light shortly after work on bank 2
Bank 2 fuel trims or catalyst monitor results implausible
c: Bank 2 sensor plugs swapped during a sensor or exhaust repair
Bank 2 sensor plugged into the bank 1 harness side
Sensor with the wrong type or cable length fitted

P241C.d: P241C is the bank 2 counterpart of P2072 and only makes sense on engines that use a separate electronic throttle per bank. The controller records that the throttle plate of that bank was frozen in place, recognised by a blade that will not follow its command in cold weather.
s: Reduced power or capped engine speed in frost
Engine will not start after a cold night
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Condensate from crankcase ventilation freezing on the throttle blade
Water or snow drawn into the intake tract
Damaged or poorly routed ventilation or make-up air hose

P241D.d: P241D marks the last step of the diesel SCR inducement: after repeated warnings about a reductant problem were ignored, the engine module blocks further engine starts. On FCA's 3.0L EcoDiesel (Ram 1500, Jeep Grand Cherokee from 2014) a DEF-related code first triggers a dash message, after 50 miles a restart countdown, and after 150 miles no restart; P241D is then stored and only sets alongside the causing code.
s: Engine will not restart, message to service the DEF system
Earlier countdown warnings in the cluster
Check engine light with further SCR codes
c: DEF tank run empty after warnings were ignored
Unrepaired SCR or DEF system fault (pump, pressure, quality, NOx sensor)
Causing code erased while the inducement remains active

P241E.d: Many SCR systems thaw frozen DEF with engine coolant routed through the tank or supply module; an electrically switched valve lets coolant in. P241E means that valve stays shut although the controller has opened it, so the expected warm-up does not appear.
s: SCR or DEF warning in cold weather, DEF does not thaw
Higher NOx, possibly further SCR codes
Countdown to restart or power limitation if left unrepaired
c: Valve seized or diaphragm stuck in the closed position
Kinked, blocked or air-locked coolant hoses to the DEF heater
Low coolant level or weak circulation

P241F.d: Engines with two EGR loops can carry two coolers; P241F flags that the second one, cooler B, no longer removes enough heat from the recirculated gas. GM's 2020 diesel tables (20OBDG04) pin cooler B to the low-pressure EGR path: efficiency is derived from the gas temperatures before and after the cooler, corrected for flow, averaged and failed below 50 percent, a Type B fault (two trips) with coolant between 60 and 13
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher NOx, possibly more frequent DPF regenerations
c: Soot or lacquer deposits on the cooler passages
Drifting EGR temperature sensor before or after the cooler
Weak coolant flow through the cooler (air pocket, thermostat, pump)

P2420.d: P2420 means the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads high - typically a short to battery voltage on the control line or an overcurrent detected by the driver stage. Karma lists P2420 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve of the Revero and GS-6, which the ECM operates, and Subaru's bulletin 09-103-23 for 2015 Legacy/Outback with an evaporative leak check module (ELCM) includes P2420 among the codes to ch
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
No noticeable driveability change
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Switching valve coil with too low resistance (overcurrent)
Faulty driver stage in the ECM

P2421.d: The vent valve closes off the evaporative system, letting a leak test hold pressure or vacuum. P2421 says the valve stays open when the controller has commanded it shut; the test then fails to seal, much like a gross leak.
s: Check engine light, no driveability change
EVAP readiness not set, leak codes possible
c: Valve seat or membrane contaminated by charcoal dust or dirt
Vent or tank isolation valve mechanically stuck open

P2422.d: P2422 is the opposite case: the vent path stays shut even with the valve commanded open, so tank pressure or vacuum cannot equalise. GM's Volt table (16OBDG01) is specific: with more than 697 Pa of pressure or vacuum in the sealed tank, the diurnal control valve is opened, and a fuel tank pressure change of less than 249 Pa within 10 s fails the test, Type B.
s: Check engine light
Fuel nozzle shuts off early when refuelling
Hissing when the fuel cap or flap is opened
c: Dust, dirt or insects blocking the canister vent tube or filter
Vent valve or tank isolation valve stuck closed
Detection logic needing an update (Hyundai 2020 Sonata)

P2423.d: Some very low emission petrol engines add a hydrocarbon trap: an adsorbing layer holds back unburned fuel during a cold start and releases it once the main catalyst has lit off. P2423 means the bank 1 trap no longer retains enough.
s: Check engine light, no noticeable driving change
Higher cold-start hydrocarbon emissions
c: Adsorber layer aged or saturated with deposits
ECM calibration affected by a manufacturer campaign (Nissan Altima SULEV)
Damage from misfires or oil consumption

P2424.d: P2424 applies the same check to the bank 2 hydrocarbon trap, so it can only appear on V or flat engines that have such a trap in each exhaust branch. No manufacturer documents P2424 publicly.
s: Check engine light
Possible failed emission inspection
c: Bank 2 adsorber layer aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 trap distorting the measurement
Thermal damage from misfires on bank 2

P2425.d: The EGR cooling valve, often a bypass flap, decides whether recirculated gas passes through the cooler or around it, for example to warm up faster. P2425 reports that the driver stage sees no load on the control line, typically an open wire, a loose connector or a burnt-out actuator.
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up or higher NOx depending on flap position
c: Broken wire in the control circuit near the hot exhaust side
Loose or corroded connector at the valve
Open coil or motor inside the valve actuator

P2426.d: P2426 is set when the command wire of the cooling valve reads too low, which on most driver stages means the wire is shorted to ground or the output cannot pull up. In Ford's Power Stroke summary the low and high faults are detected together by a short-circuit check of the cooler bypass actuator that runs all the time and fails after 2 seconds.
s: Check engine light
Bypass flap no longer moves
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve actuator
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2427.d: P2427 points to the high side: the control line of the EGR cooling valve is pulled towards battery voltage or the stage sees excessive current. VW's 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI chart (CNRB) states the criterion as a current above 2.20 A, a sign of a short in the actuator winding or wiring to supply.
s: Check engine light
Flap remains in spring position, possibly slower warm-up
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Shorted turns in the actuator, drawing excess current
Water ingress in the valve connector

P2428.d: P2428 is a protection code: the exhaust on bank 1 has become hot enough to endanger the aftertreatment, above all the diesel particulate filter. GM's 2014 diesel tables (14OBDG04) list five triggers, any of which fails the test after 6 seconds: about 800 °C ahead of the oxidation catalyst, 900 °C behind it, 800 °C behind the filter, or rises of more than 600 °C across the catalyst and 400 °C across the filter.
s: Warning lamp on immediately, often with reduced power
Strong heat or burning smell from the exhaust
Particulate filter or catalyst damage in severe cases
c: Uncontrolled soot burn in an overloaded particulate filter
Leaking injector or excessive post-injection reaching the catalyst
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high

P2429.d: P2429 reports excessive exhaust heat on bank 2 and therefore exists only on engines with two separately monitored exhaust branches, such as V diesels with an aftertreatment line per bank. No manufacturer publishes P2429.
s: Warning lamp with reduced engine power
Unusual heat or smell from one side of the exhaust
c: Excessive soot burn in the bank 2 filter
Leaking injector or misfire on bank 2 sending fuel into the exhaust
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading high

P242A.d: P242A is the general circuit code for the third exhaust temperature probe on bank 1. Where that probe sits is up to each manufacturer: VW counts it behind the oxidation catalyst on the 2014 Touareg TDI, Deutz places it downstream of the SCR catalyst on its EMR L1 controller.
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regeneration or DEF dosing suspended
Implausible or missing value for sensor 3 in the scan tool
c: Open circuit or corroded terminal in the sensor connector or harness near the exhaust
Ground fault or sensor supply out of range (failure types -F0/-1C on Deutz)
On Ford diesels, sensor reading deviating from the exhaust temperature model

P242B.d: P242B flags a reading from exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 that is electrically fine but makes no physical sense. Most checks start from a cold soak: GM's 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B) waits for more than 10,800 s engine-off and then expects the probe to warm up enough, which exposes a probe that has slipped from the gas stream or is frozen at one value (Type B).
s: MIL on, often together with P2080 or P2084
No DEF dosing or parked regeneration refused
DPF warning lamp on
c: Sensor loose or no longer reaching into the exhaust stream
Sensor drifted or stuck at one value
ECM software miscalculating soak time (Volvo/Mack 2015–2016, software update)
Sensors swapped or wrong part fitted after repair

P242C.d: P242C means the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 sits below its valid range. What that says about the wiring depends on the sensor type.
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip on GM
Sensor 3 shows an implausibly low temperature in the scan tool
Regeneration blocked, filter load rising
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground near the exhaust
Connector damaged, wet or with pushed-back terminals

P242D.d: P242D is the mirror case of P242C: bank 1 probe 3 reports more than its plausible maximum, typically because the circuit is open or touches a supply. GM's 2020 diesel tables trigger above 900 Ω after 10 of 20 samples, the 3.0 L LZO above 100 MΩ for an analog probe or above 1,289.85 °C for a digital one; both tables rate it Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first faulty trip.
s: MIL on in the first faulty trip (GM Type A)
Sensor 3 shows an implausibly high temperature or the maximum value
Regeneration and DEF dosing restricted
c: Open signal or return wire, broken by heat or vibration
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Low battery voltage during diagnosis (Ram 2025–2026 note)

P242E.d: P242E is set when exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 jumps between two samples faster than real exhaust gas can change, even though each single value is inside the valid range. GM documents this as a quick-change monitor that runs every 100 ms.
s: MIL after the second faulty trip
Sensor 3 value jumps in the scan tool live data
Code comes and goes, often after rough roads or washing
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Harness insulation damaged by exhaust heat, intermittent contact

P242F.d: P242F reports that so much incombustible ash has collected in the bank 1 particulate filter that it restricts flow and no regeneration can clear it. Ash comes mainly from oil additives, builds up over the service life and leaves the filter only through cleaning or replacement.
s: MIL or DPF service message
Regenerations becoming more frequent
Loss of power at high load due to back pressure
c: Filter has reached its ash capacity after high mileage or operating hours
High oil consumption or unsuitable oil (high ash content) speeding up ash build-up
Calibration setting the code without a defect (Ram 6.7 L 2015, bulletin 18-037-16)
Differential pressure sensor or hoses reporting too much restriction

P2430.d: On engines with an electric secondary air (AIR) pump, a pressure sensor in the duct between pump and shut-off valve tells the engine computer whether air is really moving to bank 1. P2430 is the basic signal fault of that sensor.
s: Check engine lamp after two cold starts
Secondary air readiness not set, emissions test refused
No noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Pressure sensor no longer reacts, signal frozen at one value
Sensor port or duct blocked by water, ice or debris from the pump
Corroded connector or damaged harness at the sensor

P2431.d: P2431 flags a bank 1 secondary air pressure signal that can be read but makes no sense. The usual check compares the sensor with barometric pressure: with the pump off both should agree, with the pump running the rise must stay within limits.
s: Check engine lamp, often only after cold starts
Secondary air monitor not completed
Possibly further MAP or lean codes if the reference is wrong
c: Pressure sensor drifted or reacts too slowly
Wrong barometric reference, e.g. damaged MAP sensor wiring
Restricted or leaking air duct around the sensor port

P2432.d: P2432 means the bank 1 secondary air pressure signal has fallen below its valid band – typically a broken signal lead, a ground short or a missing 5 V reference. GM's tables give the limit as under 5 % of the reference (400 failed samples out of 1,000 on the 2005 3.8L V6) and, from 2018, under 6 % for 800 of 1,000 samples; the check runs all the time and is rated Type B.
s: Check engine lamp, also while driving warm
Secondary air tests not run
Other sensor codes if the shared 5 V line is affected
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference missing, often shared with other sensors

P2433.d: With P2433 the bank 1 secondary air pressure signal sits above its upper limit, pointing to a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, an open sensor ground or a failed sensor. GM uses more than 95 % of the reference on the 2005–2006 3.8L V6, more than 94 % on the 2006 Corvette and CTS-V V8s and in the 2018 tables (800 of 1,000 samples), always as a Type B fault watched without a break.
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Secondary air readiness stays incomplete
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal

P2434.d: P2434 is meant for a bank 1 secondary air pressure sensor whose signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing for good – typically a loose connector pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for example, covers the same sensor with P2430–P2433 only and folds signal noise into its stuck-in-range and performance checks.
s: Check engine lamp that comes and goes
Fault often not reproducible in the workshop
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor plug
Chafed or heat-damaged wire near engine or exhaust

P2435.d: P2435 is the bank 2 version of the basic signal fault of the secondary air pressure sensor. It exists only where each cylinder bank has its own air path with a sensor, for instance Audi's R8 V10 with the bank 2 sensor G610.
s: Check engine lamp after cold starts
Secondary air readiness not reached
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor no longer reacts
Plug or harness on the bank 2 side damaged
Sensor port blocked by moisture or debris

P2436.d: P2436 says the bank 2 secondary air pressure reading is electrically valid but does not match what the system expects. Audi documents the code on the 2017 R8 and R8 Spyder V10: bulletin 2049142 (TSB group 01, 18-56) pairs P243600 with P243700 and has the bank 2 pressure sensor G610 replaced, following the guided fault finding.
s: Check engine lamp
Often stored together with P2437
Secondary air readiness incomplete
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor drifted or failed (Audi R8 replaces G610)
Sensing port or hose on bank 2 clogged or leaking

P2437.d: P2437 reports a bank 2 secondary air pressure signal stuck below its valid range. Audi lists it for the 2017 R8 and R8 Spyder, where it often shows up together with P2436; the bulletin's remedy is a new bank 2 pressure sensor G610.
s: Check engine lamp
Secondary air tests on both banks suspended
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor failed (Audi R8 bulletin replaces G610)
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V supply to the sensor missing

P2438.d: P2438 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2433: the secondary air pressure signal of the second bank reads above its upper limit. GM mentions P2438 next to P2437 among the codes that block its AIR sensor and flow tests in the 2018 tables, but publishes no row of its own for it, because the engines described there have one air path.
s: Check engine lamp
Secondary air readiness stays incomplete
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or supply voltage
Open ground circuit of the bank 2 sensor

P2439.d: P2439 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the bank 2 secondary air pressure signal. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the description rests on CARB's demand that every electrical AIR component be checked for circuit faults and rationality, together with the bank 2 sensor layout known from Audi's R8 V10 (sensor G610).
s: Warning lamp appears now and then
Code returns after clearing without visible cause
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the bank 2 sensor
Harness near the exhaust side brittle or chafed

P243A.d: P243A is the bank 2 counterpart of P242F: the ash load in the second particulate filter has grown so large that the filter chokes the exhaust and must be cleaned or replaced. A bank 2 filter only exists where each cylinder bank of a V engine feeds its own filter strand.
s: MIL or filter service message
Higher fuel consumption from frequent regenerations
Reduced power at high load
c: Bank 2 filter full of ash after long service
Oil burning on bank 2 (valve stem seals, turbo seal) adding ash
Bank 2 pressure sensor or hose reporting too much restriction

P243B.d: P243B means the second particulate filter is so restricted that the engine controller cuts power to protect engine and filter. Ford documents the code in its 2024–2025 OBD summary for gasoline engines, as part of the petrol particulate filter monitor next to P246C for bank 1.
s: Noticeably reduced engine power
MIL on
Poor acceleration at higher speed
c: Bank 2 filter overloaded with soot or ash
Damaged or blocked exhaust pipe on bank 2
Pressure sensor or hose on bank 2 reporting too high a pressure

P243C.d: P243C is stored when the bank 2 particulate filter needs regeneration more often than its calibration allows. CARB requires diesel OBD to recognise regeneration so frequent that emissions would rise above the limit.
s: Regeneration running unusually often
Higher fuel consumption, rising oil level
MIL on
c: Too much soot from bank 2 cylinders (injector, EGR or boost fault)
Pressure sensor or hose overstating the bank 2 soot load
Filter partly filled with ash, leaving little soot capacity

P243D.d: P243D says that a regeneration of the bank 2 particulate filter took longer than the calibrated limit. CARB expects the OBD system to notice when a filter fails to regenerate properly under conditions in which it was designed to.
s: Regeneration seems to run for a very long time (fan, idle speed)
Higher fuel consumption
MIL on
c: Exhaust on bank 2 not reaching regeneration temperature (short trips, low load)
Oxidation catalyst on bank 2 converting too little fuel into heat
Temperature or pressure sensor giving wrong values

P243E.d: P243E is set when the second filter strand has finished regenerating but the soot was not burned off as planned. CARB requires a malfunction to be flagged whenever the filter does not regenerate properly under the manufacturer's intended conditions.
s: MIL on, filter warning
Regeneration restarts soon after the last one
Rising soot load in live data
c: Regenerations interrupted by short trips or engine shut-off
Too little heat on bank 2 (catalyst, post-injection or dosing fault)
Faulty temperature or differential pressure signal

P243F.d: P243F means the soot load estimated for the bank 2 particulate filter has climbed past the level that a normal regeneration can still handle safely. Burning off too much soot at once can overheat and crack the substrate, so many engines then block automatic regeneration and call for a service regeneration or a new filter.
s: MIL and filter warning on
Automatic regeneration blocked, service regeneration needed
Reduced power possible
c: Repeatedly aborted regenerations, short trips or long idling
Engine fault raising soot output on bank 2 (injector, EGR, boost)
Pressure sensor or hose overstating the soot load

P2440.d: P2440 means the bank 1 secondary air shut-off (switching) valve stays open when it should be closed. GM tests it in phase 2 of its air check: the pump runs while the valve is commanded shut, so pressure in the duct should build; if it stays more than 3 kPa below the model (2005–2006 3.8L V6) or under the 2018 table limit, the code sets as Type B.
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Pump noisy or failing later due to exhaust backflow
Often stored together with P2442 or P2445
c: Valve held open by debris from a damaged pump filter
Valve seat carboned up or corroded by condensate
Electric or vacuum actuator does not close the valve

P2441.d: P2441 flags a bank 1 secondary air valve that does not open when commanded, so pump air never reaches the exhaust ports. Toyota documents it on 2005–2009 4.7L V8 (2UZ-FE) models such as 4Runner, Sequoia, Tundra and Land Cruiser: bulletin T-SB-0230-12 traces it to debris from the air pump contaminating the valves and lists it next to faults of the No.
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions, failed readiness check
c: Valve seized closed by debris or corrosion
Valve actuator, control solenoid or vacuum supply faulty
Kinked or collapsed air hose downstream of the valve

P2442.d: P2442 is the stuck-open fault of the bank 2 secondary air valve: with the pump on and the valve commanded shut, air still passes, or exhaust flows back towards the pump. Lexus applies it to the 2010–2013 GX 460 with the 1UR-FE engine; bulletin L-SB-0028-14 replaces the bank 2 air switching valve and the pump, because a damaged pump filter sheds debris.
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Pump noise or later pump failure
Melted or brittle air hoses
c: Bank 2 valve held open by debris from the pump filter
Valve seat or diaphragm damaged by heat or condensate
Actuator does not close the valve

P2443.d: P2443 signals that the bank 2 secondary air valve stays shut although the engine computer commands it open, so the second bank gets no added air during warm-up. Subaru lists the code for the 2011–2015 WRX STI and recommends always following the diagnosis for the opposite bank too, since valve or hose faults on one side can show up on the other.
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Secondary air readiness not set
c: Bank 2 valve seized in the closed position
Leaking vacuum line or faulty control solenoid
Kinked air hose on the bank 2 side

P2444.d: P2444 means the secondary air pump keeps blowing after the engine computer has switched it off. GM checks this in phase 3 of its sequence, with the pump commanded off and the valve closed: if duct pressure stays higher than predicted – by more than 1.5 kPa within 5 s on the 2005–2006 3.8L V6, by more than 4.2 kPa within 10 s for the 2006 V8s in Corvette and CTS-V – the code sets as Type A and lights the MIL on the fi
s: Check engine lamp on the first trip
Pump audibly running long after start or with engine off
Discharged battery
c: Pump relay contacts welded or sticking
Relay control circuit shorted to power
Output driver in the engine computer faulty

P2445.d: P2445 reports that the secondary air pump delivers no air although it is commanded on. Toyota and Lexus use it on several trucks: on 2UZ-FE 4.7L models (T-SB-0230-12, revised in 2013 to include P2445), on the 2010–2013 GX 460 (L-SB-0028-14) and on the 2012 Tacoma with the 1GR-FE (T-SB-0033-17).
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
No pump noise directly after a cold start
Often stored together with P0418
c: Pump seized by moisture or debris from a damaged filter
Blown pump fuse or failed pump relay
Open pump supply or ground, corroded plug

P2446.d: P2446 is the bank 2 entry for a secondary air pump that keeps running after being switched off. The code is meaningful only on engines with a separate pump per cylinder bank or where the system reports pump faults per bank; no manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine lamp
Pump keeps humming after the warm-up phase
c: Relay of the bank 2 pump stuck closed
Faulty output driver in the engine computer

P2447.d: P2447 indicates that the bank 2 secondary air pump does not deliver air when commanded. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; Toyota and Lexus, whose V6 and V8 trucks feed both banks from one pump through two valves, log a dead pump as P2445.
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Readiness for secondary air not set
c: Bank 2 pump seized after water ingress
Blown fuse or failed relay of the bank 2 pump
Corroded pump connector or open ground

P2448.d: P2448 means more secondary air reaches bank 1 than the system expects – for example when the shut-off valve leaks, the pump keeps blowing, or the control logic sees a stronger lean shift than modelled. Ford uses the code: its 2012 OBD summary names P0491, P0410 and P2448 as the bank 1 codes behind the secondary air readiness and in-use monitor counters, and Ford's 2014 code list (published for the Boss 302S) marks P2
s: Check engine lamp
Lean-running codes or fuel trim deviation after cold start
c: Shut-off valve does not seal fully
Pump relay sticks, pump runs longer than commanded
Leaking check valve in the air path

P2449.d: P2449 is the bank 2 high-flow fault of the AIR system: during or after the air injection phase the second bank receives more air than predicted. Ford assigns it in its 2012 OBD summary to the bank 2 secondary air readiness, next to P0492 for too little flow, so the code belongs to Ford's AIR monitor even though no threshold is published.
s: Check engine lamp
Usually no change in driving behaviour
c: Bank 2 shut-off valve does not seal
Pump keeps running due to a sticking relay

P244A.d: P244A means the pressure difference across the bank 1 particulate filter is lower than exhaust flow and soot load predict. That points to a damaged or removed substrate or, far more often, to a pressure line that has slipped off, split or clogged.
s: MIL on in the first faulty trip
Soot load shown near zero, regeneration not triggered
Visible smoke if the substrate is damaged
c: Upstream pressure hose disconnected, split or blocked
Differential pressure sensor reading too low (Ford 6.7 L, Land Rover TDV6 bulletins)
Filter substrate cracked, melted or removed

P244B.d: P244B reports a pressure drop across the bank 1 particulate filter that is too large for the current exhaust flow. On GM's 3.0 L LZO the same monitor also catches a leaking or disconnected downstream pipe: depending on the sensor type it compares either the downstream pressure with a limit or the pressure-to-flow ratio, as a Type A code.
s: MIL on, often with reduced power
High soot level indication in the cluster
Regeneration requested repeatedly
c: Filter heavily loaded with soot or ash
Downstream pressure hose leaking or disconnected (GM LZO)
Water in the differential pressure sensor after washing (GM L5P 2025)
ECM calibration overstating soot load (Cadillac XT4 diesel, update)

P244C.d: During an active regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature with late injections so the soot in the particulate filter can burn. P244C is stored when bank 1 does not get hot enough or does not stay hot long enough.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and particulate filter warning on
Regenerations noticeably frequent or never finishing
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded
c: Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the post-injected fuel does not light off
Regenerations repeatedly cut short by short trips, idling or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of catalyst or filter reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the catalyst cooling the gas

P244D.d: This is the overheating side of the bank 1 regeneration check. While soot is being burned off, the controller keeps exhaust temperature inside a window; if it climbs past the upper limit, the substrate and the oxidation catalyst risk cracking or melting, so the burn is stopped and P244D is logged.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration aborted, filter warning stays on
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment
c: Too much fuel reaching the exhaust (leaking injector or aftertreatment doser)
Heavily overloaded filter burning off too fast
Exhaust temperature sensor or its wiring giving implausibly high readings

P244E.d: P244E only exists on engines that have a separate particulate filter for the second cylinder bank, which is rare. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it mirrors P244C, so the logic described for bank 1 applies here.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter warning, regeneration does not complete
c: Bank 2 oxidation catalyst no longer converting post-injected fuel
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading low
Driving pattern too short for a complete regeneration
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the catalyst

P244F.d: The bank 2 counterpart of P244D: during a filter burn the second bank's exhaust gets hotter than the substrate tolerates. No manufacturer documents P244F publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration stopped, possibly reduced power
c: Surplus fuel on bank 2 from a leaking injector
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor or wiring reading too high
Bank 2 filter heavily overloaded before the burn

P2450.d: The switching valve sits in the evaporative system and either seals off part of it during the leak test or redirects flow; P2450 means the valve does not do its job or remains open. Ford calls it the vapor blocking valve: in 2020 to 2024 gasoline models the check runs in the third phase of the 0.040 inch cruise leak test, lasts 2 to 3 s and fails when a calculated ratio stays below 2.75 (Mode 6 test $3D, component $8
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, usually no noticeable driving change
Possible fuel odor near the tank area
c: Switching valve sticking open or not sealing
Internal fault of a leak detection pump that houses the valve
Monitor software needing an update (known on some Ford trucks)
Cracked or loose vapor hose at the valve

P2451.d: P2451 is the reverse fault of P2450: the evaporative system switching valve will not open when commanded, so vapor or test pressure cannot pass where the system expects it. It shows up mainly on vehicles with a sealed, pressurized fuel tank, such as plug-in hybrids.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel door or refueling release slow or not working on sealed-tank hybrids
c: Tank shutter or switching valve stuck closed
Fuel tank pressure sensor giving wrong values to the monitor
Software or test-sequence issue (fuel door handling on some hybrids)

P2452.d: The pressure sensor A of the particulate filter, usually a differential sensor with hoses to the filter inlet and outlet, tells the ECM how loaded the filter is. Despite its generic circuit title, P2452 is in practice an offset check made when no exhaust flows.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration too early, too late or inhibited
c: Sensor offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Sensor hose blocked by soot or condensate

P2453.d: P2453 means the particulate filter pressure signal is electrically fine but does not behave like a real filter pressure. Manufacturers use two kinds of test.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning, regeneration inhibited or too frequent
Reduced power on some vehicles
c: Sensor hose disconnected, split, kinked or blocked
Sensor skewed or stuck, for example from moisture ingress
High resistance in sensor wiring or ECM grounds

P2454.d: The particulate filter pressure sensor is a three-wire part: the ECM feeds it 5 V and ground and reads a signal that rises with the pressure difference across the filter. P2454 means that signal sits below the lowest plausible value.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning or regeneration inhibited
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector unplugged
Internal sensor failure, for example from moisture
5 V reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply

P2455.d: P2455 means the particulate filter pressure sensor signal sits above the highest plausible value, at the top of the 5 V range. Ford's 2023 diesels and the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) both use 4.9 V as the limit, Ford within 2 s and Saab after 1 s; on Ford's 6.7 L the signal follows roughly 0.082 V per kPa above 0.45 V, so 4.9 V would be about 54 kPa.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning or regeneration inhibited
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2456.d: Here the pressure sensor A signal is within range but jumps in a way no real exhaust flow could cause. GM's 2017 and 2018 diesels compare each raw sample with the one before; a step larger than 20 % repeated over 80 or 160 samples sets the code after two trips, but only if no electrical fault is present.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration started at odd times or blocked
c: Loose or corroded sensor connector terminals
Harness chafing or heat damage near the exhaust
Condensate in the sensor or its pressure hoses

P2457.d: The EGR cooler is supposed to bring recirculated exhaust close to coolant temperature; P2457 says cooler A no longer removes enough heat, as CARB requires diesel systems to detect. GM rates efficiency as the drop across the cooler divided by the gap between inlet gas and coolant; in the 2017 tables the Duramax fails below 60 %, the MDE engine family below 50 %, each after two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher NOx, sometimes reduced EGR or power
Coolant loss or white smoke if the cooler is also leaking
c: Cooler passages fouled with soot and lacquer
Bypass flap stuck in bypass position or bypass module loose
EGR outlet temperature sensor reading too high
Low coolant level or poor coolant flow through the cooler
Monitor software misjudging efficiency (known on some trucks)

P2458.d: During a regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature, mostly by late post-injection burned in the oxidation catalyst, until the soot in the particulate filter oxidises. P2458 means a regeneration took longer than the calibrated limit, so the filter was not cleaned in the expected time.
s: DPF warning or MIL, depending on the manufacturer
Cooling fan and raised idle running on after shutdown
Higher fuel consumption
c: ECM calibration that needs an update (documented by Volkswagen)
Short trips that keep regenerations from finishing
Oxidation catalyst too weak to reach regeneration temperature

P2459.d: P2459 means the particulate filter is being regenerated more often than the calibration expects. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag regeneration so frequent that emissions would exceed the limit; frequent regeneration also dilutes oil and costs fuel.
s: MIL or DPF warning
Higher fuel consumption and rising oil level
Reduced engine power if the fault persists
c: High soot output from the engine (injectors, EGR, air leaks)
Differential pressure reading too high (sensor, blocked or swapped hoses)
Filter loaded with ash or defective from manufacture

P245A.d: The bypass lets cold-start EGR skip the cooler and is switched back to cooling once the engine is warm. P245A flags the bank 1 control circuit, usually as an open.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR cooler bypass no longer switching; possible P2457 or P24A5 as follow-up
c: Open wire or unplugged connector at the bypass actuator
Actuator motor or solenoid winding open
Control software needing an update (some Ford diesels)

P245B.d: P245B is set when the bank 1 bypass is electrically intact but does not reach or hold the commanded position, or when switching it has no visible thermal effect. GM's 2017 Duramax with a position-controlled DC-motor flap compares setpoint and feedback; a tracking error above 16 % in 1280 of 1600 samples, with a steady setpoint, coolant over 70 °C and outside air above minus 23 °C, sets a Type B fault, and P24A5 follo
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Longer warm-up or higher NOx when the bypass stays in one position
c: Bypass flap or shaft sticking from carbon deposits
Weak vacuum supply or leaking hose on vacuum-operated bypass
Slow EGR temperature sensor after the cooler

P245C.d: P245C reports that the control line of the bank 1 bypass actuator is pulled toward ground. GM documents this in its diesel tables: in 2014 the driver stage detects low voltage while it is switched off and treats it as a ground short, and in the 2017 tables the vacuum-switched bypass fails when the resistance to ground drops below 0.5 Ohm in 24 of 30 samples, rated Type B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bypass stuck in one position, possibly with EGR cooler efficiency code
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion bridging connector pins

P245D.d: P245D is the short-to-supply case of the bank 1 bypass circuit. For the Duramax with a DC-motor bypass, GM's 2017 tables watch the current through the H-bridge while it drives the flap: more than 8 A in 160 of 200 samples sets a Type B fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bypass actuator switched off by the controller and left in default position
c: Control software reporting a false actuator fault (known on some Ram diesels)
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Actuator motor drawing excessive current (low-resistance winding, binding)

P245E.d: Which sensor is B depends on the maker. Ford's 2013 6.7 L Power Stroke has an exhaust pressure sensor ahead of the filter as A and a two-port differential sensor across it as B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Soot load estimate unreliable, regeneration timing affected
c: Sensor B offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Pressure hose kinked or blocked so pressure is trapped
Wiring or connector fault on the sensor B circuit

P245F.d: With P245F the controller decides that the sensor B value is electrically fine but makes no physical sense. Ford's 2024 gasoline strategy runs three such tests on the B sensor of the gasoline particulate filter: an offset check with the engine stopped that fails once the average reaches 16 to 32 hPa; a rationality check that fails when the reading stays at or above the pressure expected for the current exhaust flow f
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter regeneration triggered too early, too late or blocked
c: Sensor B hose cracked, disconnected or blocked
Condensate in the pressure line falsifying the reading
Sensor B drifted out of calibration
Control software needing an update (some Jeep models)

P2460.d: P2460 means the analog output of pressure sensor B has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. On Ford's 2013 6.7 L diesel, sensor B is the differential pressure sensor across the filter; its output runs from about 0.45 V at zero to roughly 4.8 V near 38 kPa, and anything under 0.10 V for 2 s with the key on, battery between 9 and 16.25 V, sets the code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration based on a model only, possibly more frequent
c: 5 V reference to sensor B missing or shorted
Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck low

P2461.d: When pressure sensor B reports a voltage above its usable range, P2461 is stored. Ford sets the limit at 4.90 V for 2 s on the 2013 6.7 L diesel, where B is the differential sensor across the filter, and at 4.73 V for 5 s on the 2024 gasoline particulate filters.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because the filter appears heavily loaded
c: Condensate in the sensor tubes producing false high readings
Sensor ground open or signal shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck high

P2462.d: P2462 covers a sensor B signal that drops out or jumps for short moments without staying outside its range long enough for the low or high codes. Ford is the only maker found documenting it: the 2024 gasoline particulate filter summary lists P2462 next to P2460 and P2461 in the continuously running analog circuit check, with about 5 s needed to register a fault, and no separate threshold is published.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only after rough roads or rain
Pressure reading jumping in live data
c: Terminal losing contact under engine vibration
Harness rubbing on a bracket or exhaust part

P2463.d: P2463 means the soot load in the particulate filter has passed the level at which the engine still regenerates it on its own. GM's 2009 Duramax sets it at 70 g or more for 5 minutes, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel at more than 32 g for 30 s, both as Type A codes; GM's 2018 diesels use the pressure-based soot model with 120 failures in 150 samples.
s: DPF full or exhaust filter message in the cluster
MIL on and reduced engine power
Higher fuel consumption
c: Regenerations not completed because of short trips or long idling
Differential pressure sensor, its hoses or wiring reading too high
Fault that prevents regeneration (fuel doser, temperature sensor)

P2464.d: P2464 is stored when the pressure drop across the second particulate filter stays smaller than the controller predicts for the current exhaust flow. Only engines that run a separate filter on each bank, typically larger V diesels, can log it.
s: MIL on
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is damaged
Regeneration suspended or reduced power on some engines
c: Pressure sensing hose of the bank 2 filter detached, cracked or leaking
Upstream sensing port or line blocked with soot or condensate
Filter substrate cracked, melted or removed

P2465.d: P2465 means the second particulate filter builds up more back pressure than the controller accepts for the exhaust flow it calculates. The code is only possible where each cylinder bank has its own filter.
s: MIL on
Frequent or prolonged regeneration attempts
Loss of power, possibly limp mode
c: Bank 2 filter heavily loaded with soot or ash
Downstream sensing hose blocked, kinked or swapped
Dented or obstructed exhaust pipe behind the filter

P2466.d: P2466 is the general circuit code for the third exhaust temperature probe in the bank 2 exhaust path, so it only appears on engines with two separate aftertreatment lines. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: MIL on
Implausible or missing value for this probe in live data
Filter regeneration or DEF dosing suspended
c: Temperature probe failed internally or open
Connector or wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream

P2467.d: P2467 means the third exhaust temperature probe on bank 2 delivers an electrically valid signal that does not match the operating state. A public threshold for this exact code is not available.
s: MIL on
Temperature value lags or deviates from neighbouring probes
White smoke and coolant loss if the EGR cooler leaks
c: Probe aged, drifting or frozen at one value
Probe loose or pulled out of the gas stream
Coolant entering the exhaust through a leaking EGR cooler (Ford 2.0 L EcoBoost)
Controller software judging the probe too strictly

P2468.d: P2468 reports that probe 3 in the bank 2 exhaust line delivers a signal below the lowest value the input can produce with an intact circuit. With the usual resistive probes this nearly always means the signal line or the sensor itself has a ground short.
s: MIL on
Probe shows an implausible value at a standstill
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Connector melted or with water ingress

P2469.d: P2469 is logged when bank 2 probe number 3 pushes its input above the permitted ceiling. An unplugged connector, a broken wire or a burnt-out sensing element produces exactly that, as does a signal line shorted to a voltage source.
s: MIL on, often already in the first trip
Probe shows a maximum or invalid value
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited
c: Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source

P246A.d: P246A flags a third bank 2 exhaust temperature probe whose reading jumps from sample to sample faster than real gas temperature could, even though every single value stays inside the legal range. The bank 2 code itself is not described by any manufacturer in public material.
s: MIL on after a repeated fault
Temperature trace jumps in live data
Fault may come and go with bumps or engine heat
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Harness strands broken by heat and vibration
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact

P246B.d: P246B says the controller wanted to clean the particulate filter but the vehicle did not offer the conditions its strategy needs, for example enough exhaust heat, a long enough run or a functioning air path. It describes a failed or blocked regeneration request rather than a defective part on its own, so the real cause is usually stored beside it.
s: Regeneration does not start or is aborted repeatedly
Filter warning or rising soot load
MIL on together with the root-cause code on some vehicles
c: Another stored fault (e.g. intake throttle, sensors) blocking regeneration
Failed intake air shutoff throttle (Land Rover TDV6)
Short trips or long idling without enough exhaust heat

P246C.d: P246C is the final stage of the bank 1 filter loading monitor: the filter is judged so clogged that the controller reduces engine output to protect engine and filter. Ford uses it on diesels with an immediate MIL plus wrench light.
s: MIL and service or wrench light on
Marked loss of power (limp mode)
Drive-to-clean or filter full message
c: Soot overload after repeatedly missed or aborted regenerations
Mostly stationary or low-speed operation without full regenerations
Filter at the end of its life with high ash content
PCM calibration overestimating soot load (Ford bulletins)

P246D.d: P246D compares two pressure readings at the particulate filter that ought to agree under steady conditions. Which sensor is A and which is B is decided by each manufacturer.
s: MIL on
Regeneration too early, too late or suspended
Pressure values of the two sensors disagree in live data
c: Sensing hoses swapped, kinked or leaking
Water or soot in a sensing line
One pressure sensor drifting out of calibration

P246E.d: P246E is the general code for the fourth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1, usually the last one in the aftertreatment line. Ford's diesels give it a model check rather than an electrical one: after a cold start the measured EGT14 value may differ from the modelled temperature by no more than 80 °C, the comparison lasting 200 to 400 s and the deviation having to persist for 20 s.
s: MIL on
Value of the last exhaust probe deviates from expectation
Regeneration or DEF dosing suspended
c: Probe aged or failed, reading far from the model
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Exhaust leak near the probe cooling the reading

P246F.d: P246F stands for a fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe whose signal is electrically fine but physically implausible. Both main users test it after a long soak.
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Probe disagrees with neighbouring temperatures after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Probe stuck at one value or drifting
Probe loose or backed out of the exhaust pipe
Probe connectors swapped with a neighbouring sensor

P2470.d: P2470 means the signal of bank 1 probe number 4 has dropped below its valid floor, which on resistive probes indicates a short to ground. Ford's diesels flag a voltage under 0.10 V with the key on and 9 to 16.25 V supply, checked continuously over about 2 s.
s: MIL on
Implausible value for the last exhaust probe
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Low battery voltage during diagnosis distorting readings (Ram)

P2471.d: P2471 is set when the fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe drives its input above the upper limit, the picture of an open circuit, an unplugged sensor or a short to voltage. Ford's diesels call more than 2.66 V a fault.
s: MIL on, on GM possibly in the first trip
Last exhaust probe shows maximum or substitute value
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited
c: Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source

P2472.d: P2472 reports that the last bank 1 temperature probe (sensor 4) changes its signal too abruptly between two readings, although each reading on its own lies in range. GM documents it as a quick-change monitor with a 100 ms task: the 2017 and 2018 diesel tables look at the resistance step between consecutive samples (more than 10 Ω) and fail after 15 of 30 samples, the 2025 tables use a temperature step above 100 °C wi
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Temperature value flickers in live data
Fault comes and goes, often after rough roads
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Wire fatigue near the hot exhaust pipe
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact

P2473.d: P2473 covers the wiring of probe number four in the bank 2 exhaust line as a whole, so it only occurs on engines with two separate exhaust paths and a long sensor chain on each. The controller sets it when the probe line delivers a value it cannot assign to a clean low or high fault, for instance an open circuit or a sensor reporting an internal error.
s: MIL on
No usable value for bank 2 probe 4 in live data
Filter regeneration suspended
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the bank 2 probe
Fault in the control unit input stage

P2474.d: P2474 flags a plausibility problem: the electrical signal of bank 2 probe 4 is valid, yet the temperature it reports does not fit what the engine controller expects. Typical tests compare the probe with its neighbours after a long soak, when all should read about ambient, or with a modelled value during driving.
s: MIL on after repeated detection
Probe 4 of bank 2 differs clearly from the other probes after a cold soak
Regenerations incomplete or more frequent
c: Probe aged and reading off by a constant amount
Exhaust leak upstream of the probe falsifying the reading

P2475.d: P2475 is stored when the voltage from bank 2 probe 4 falls below the lowest value the probe can produce in normal use. With the resistive PTC probes common on diesels this points to a short between signal and ground, or to a sensor shorted internally.
s: MIL on
Bank 2 probe 4 shows an implausibly cold or fixed value
Regeneration or DEF dosing restricted
c: Signal wire rubbed through against the exhaust or body
Water in the connector bridging the pins

P2476.d: P2476 covers the opposite end of the scale from P2475: the signal of bank 2 probe 4 sits above its usable ceiling. Because the probe forms a voltage divider with a pull-up resistor in the control unit, an interrupted wire, a disconnected plug or a short to a supply voltage all drive the input high.
s: MIL on
Probe reads maximum or an implausibly hot value
Regeneration blocked
c: Open signal or ground wire, often heat-damaged
Connector loose or not locked after service work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P2477.d: P2477 targets a signal from bank 2 probe 4 that jumps around, while each individual sample may still be in range. Real exhaust temperature changes only gradually because the probe and pipe have thermal mass, so sudden steps between consecutive readings betray a wiring or contact issue.
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Value of bank 2 probe 4 jumps in live data
Fault code returns after being cleared
c: Loose or corroded pins in the probe connector
Wire strands breaking near the hot pipe
Cracked probe element with unstable contact

P2478.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P2478 judges the temperature itself at the first exhaust probe of bank 1, usually ahead of the oxidation catalyst. Ford's 2015 diesel summary for the 6.7L and 3.2L engines groups it with the EGT circuit check: the test is high-side only and trips at roughly 1150 °C, because the PTC probe curve leaves no separate low threshold.
s: MIL on
Power reduced to protect the exhaust parts
Smoke or a hot smell from the exhaust in real overheating
c: Real overheating from excess fuel or a leaking injector
Overly sensitive diagnosis needing a software update (VW Passat 2012)
Probe reading too high due to ageing
Lack of air from a boost leak or turbocharger fault

P2479.d: P2479 applies the same temperature-limit idea to the second bank 1 probe. On the 2015 Ford 6.7L layout this is EGT12 at the oxidation catalyst outlet, where the exotherm of a regeneration shows up first, so a runaway burn or excessive post-injection can push the reading towards the limit.
s: MIL on
Regeneration aborted
Reduced power
c: Excessive heat during regeneration, e.g. too much post-injection
Leaking injector adding unburnt fuel to the catalyst

P247A.d: P247A is the out-of-range verdict for the third bank 1 probe, which sits further down the aftertreatment line. It is the best documented code of this series.
s: MIL on
Filter regeneration aborted or repeated
Emergency mode with reduced power possible
c: Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Regeneration not reaching target temperature (VW low-side check)

P247B.d: P247B concerns the last probe in the bank 1 chain. In Ford's 2015 6.7L overview that is EGT14, mounted downstream of the particulate filter, so it sees the heat that leaves the filter during regeneration.
s: MIL on
Regeneration stopped, filter load warning possible
Power reduction
c: Thermal runaway in the particulate filter
Unburnt fuel reaching the filter from injectors or a dosing valve

P247C.d: P247C is the bank 2 counterpart of P2478: the first exhaust probe on the second cylinder bank reports a temperature outside its permitted window, typically next to the turbine outlet or catalyst inlet of that bank. It needs a V engine with separate exhaust paths and its own probe per bank.
s: MIL on
Reduced power to protect the exhaust
Bank 2 probe reads clearly above bank 1
c: Bank 2 running hot from extra fuel or a faulty injector
Air shortage on bank 2 from a boost leak or turbo fault

P247D.d: P247D applies to the second probe on bank 2, by analogy with P2479 normally downstream of that bank's oxidation catalyst, where the heat released by burning fuel during a regeneration is measured. It is set when the reported temperature leaves the plausible window, in practice mostly on the high side.
s: MIL on
Regeneration cancelled
Bank 2 probe 2 differs from its bank 1 twin
c: Too much heat in the bank 2 catalyst during regeneration
Probe reading high even on a cold engine

P247E.d: P247E does not question the wiring but the value itself: the third exhaust probe on cylinder bank 2 reports a temperature the engine control unit will not accept, in practice mostly an implausibly hot one. The code only makes sense on a V engine whose two banks keep separate exhaust paths up to the third measuring point.
s: Warning lamp on, regeneration may be aborted
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment
c: Uncontrolled soot burn or too much post-injection fuel on bank 2
Probe drifted and reports values too high
Leaking injector or turbo oil leak on bank 2

P247F.d: P247F flags an unacceptable reading from the fourth exhaust temperature probe of bank 2, the position that on most layouts sits behind the particulate filter. A genuine reading near the limit there means heat is leaving the filter, which points to a runaway regeneration.
s: Engine warning lamp lit
Regeneration blocked or power limited
c: Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Probe ageing with readings drifting upwards
Probe swapped with another position after a repair

P2480.d: P2480 is the general circuit or open-circuit fault of a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1. Five probes in one line are rare; GM's small diesels with oxidation catalyst, SCR, second catalyst and filter are among the few layouts that use them.
s: Warning lamp on
Missing or frozen value for probe 5 in live data
Filter regeneration may be suppressed
c: Broken or chafed lead to probe 5
Corroded or loose connector near the exhaust
Measuring element of the probe burned through

P2481.d: P2481 means the signal of the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe has dropped below its lower electrical limit, which on a resistive probe usually indicates a short to ground. GM documents it codegenau for its diesel ECMs: the 2017 and 2020 tables fail a probe resistance under 158 Ω, the 2018 table under 500 Ω, each after 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms, as a Type B fault.
s: Engine warning lamp after two trips
Probe 5 reads implausibly in live data
c: Signal lead chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the probe after heat damage
Neighbouring probe replaced because positions were confused

P2482.d: With P2482 the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe delivers a signal above its upper electrical limit. On GM diesels this code also covers the open circuit: the 2018 table sets it above 1400 Ω, both as a short to power with the driver off and as an interruption with the driver on, after 10 of 20 samples, Type B.
s: Warning lamp, on GM from 2020 after a single trip
Probe 5 shows a fixed extreme value
Regeneration suppressed
c: Broken lead from heat or vibration

P2483.d: P2483 is the plausibility test for the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe: the circuit is electrically fine, but the reading does not behave like a real exhaust temperature. GM's 2025 diesel tables describe the check in detail.
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Probe 5 barely changes while the other probes heat up
c: Probe not fully seated in its boss after exhaust work
Probe output stuck or responding too slowly
Heavily sooted probe tip insulating the element

P2484.d: P2484 catches a fifth bank 1 exhaust probe whose signal jumps faster than any real exhaust temperature can change. GM's diesel ECMs compare consecutive samples taken every 100 ms.
s: Warning lamp, sometimes going out again
Erratic jumps of probe 5 in live data
c: Intermittent contact in the probe connector
Harness insulation worn by heat or rubbing

P2485.d: P2485 reports a circuit or open-circuit fault at a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 2. That requires a V engine with two separate aftertreatment lines carrying five probes each, a layout no public maker document shows.
s: Warning lamp on
No valid value for this probe
c: Interrupted lead between control unit and probe
Connector left unplugged after exhaust work

P2486.d: P2486 is set when the signal of the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe sits below its lower electrical limit, typically because the lead or the probe itself shorts to ground. No manufacturer documents P2486 publicly; it presupposes two exhaust banks with five probes each.
s: Engine warning lamp
Implausible reading of this probe
c: Lead insulation damaged and touching ground

P2487.d: With P2487 the control unit sees the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe above its upper electrical limit, the picture of a short to supply voltage or, on many designs, of an open circuit. There is no public maker document for P2487.
s: Warning lamp after one trip
Probe shows maximum or no value
c: Signal lead shorted to a supply line

P2488.d: P2488 is the rationality check for the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe: the signal is electrically valid but does not follow the operating state. No manufacturer documents P2488; a second bank with five probes is unknown in public maker material.
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Regeneration may be inhibited
c: Probe not reaching into the gas flow
Exhaust leak cooling the measuring point

P2489.d: P2489 points to an unsteady signal from the fifth exhaust probe on bank 2: the value stays within its electrical limits but jumps or drops out briefly. This code is not documented by any manufacturer, as no public layout carries five probes per bank on a twin-bank engine.
s: Warning lamp coming and going
Jumping value in live data

P248A.d: P248A concerns the sense line with which the control unit measures the supply voltage reaching DEF heater A, and reports that voltage as too low. GM uses it on its diesels with an SCR power module for the tank heater: the 2016 to 2018 tables subtract the heater supply voltage from system voltage and fail a gap of more than 3 V while heating is commanded, after 10 of 12 checks at 500 ms; cranking is excluded and a los
s: Warning lamp or DEF system message
Frozen DEF not thawed in winter, dosing delayed
c: Corroded heater supply connector at the tank
Worn heater relay contact causing voltage drop
Weak battery or charging fault during heating

P248B.d: P248B is the upper counterpart to P248A: the sense signal for the supply of DEF heater A reads higher than permitted, for example when the line shorts to battery voltage, when the supply stays live although the heater is switched off, or when the sense input itself fails. No manufacturer documents P248B in public material.
s: Warning lamp
Possible battery drain if the heater stays powered
c: Sense lead shorted to battery voltage
Faulty sense input in the control module

P248C.d: P248C reports too little voltage on the sense circuit of DEF heater B. In GM's diesel tables from 2016 to 2018 heater B is the line heater, i.e.
s: DEF warning or engine lamp
Dosing faults at low temperatures
c: Corroded plug at the heated DEF line
Voltage drop across fuse or relay of the line heater
Damaged supply lead along the frame

P248D.d: P248D means the heater B sense input reads too high, typically the heated line. Possible pictures are a sense wire shorted to battery positive, a supply that remains on after the heater has been switched off, or a faulty input stage.
s: Warning lamp
Battery discharging while parked
c: Sense wire shorted to battery positive
Defective input stage in the module

P248E.d: P248E is the bank 2 counterpart of P245A: the engine controller sees no proper load on the output that drives the EGR cooler bypass of the second cylinder bank, most often because the circuit is open. Only engines with a separate EGR path per bank can set it, which in practice means V engines with two coolers.
s: Check engine light on
Longer warm-up or higher NOx on one bank because the bypass stays put
c: Unplugged connector or broken wire at the bank 2 bypass actuator
Open motor or solenoid winding in the bank 2 actuator
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P248F.d: With P248F the bank 2 bypass circuit is electrically sound, yet the flap does not do what the controller asks: it lags behind the setpoint, stops short of its end position or switching shows no effect on the gas temperature after the cooler. No manufacturer publishes a bank 2 version of this check.
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving
c: Bypass flap on bank 2 sluggish from soot and carbon
Leaking vacuum line or weak vacuum on pneumatic actuators

P2490.d: P2490 means the drive line of the bank 2 cooler bypass actuator sits too close to ground potential, typically a grounded wire between controller and actuator. It mirrors P245C on bank 1.
