s: Check engine light on
Bypass on bank 2 stuck in one mode, possibly followed by cooler efficiency codes
c: Drive wire rubbed through and touching engine ground
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 actuator connector

P2491.d: P2491 reports excess voltage or excess current in the drive circuit feeding the bypass actuator on bank 2, the classic sign of a short to supply or of a winding whose resistance has collapsed. It is the bank 2 sibling of P245D, and no maker publishes its own description of it.
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap on bank 2 rests in its default position
c: Control wire touching a battery or ignition feed
Actuator winding with too low resistance or seized motor
Controller software reporting a false actuator fault

P2492.d: The position sensor tells the controller where the bank 1 cooler bypass flap actually is; position-controlled flaps cannot be regulated without it. P2492 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the fault cannot be classed as a short to ground or to the supply.
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap no longer position-controlled
c: Damaged sensor wiring near hot exhaust parts
Loose or corroded connector at the bypass valve
5 V sensor supply missing or shared circuit shorted

P2493.d: P2493 is a plausibility fault: the bank 1 bypass position signal stays inside its electrical limits, but its value or behaviour does not fit the commanded flap position or the learned end stops. GM names the code in preliminary bulletin PI1449 for the 2015 Silverado and Sierra with the LML Duramax, where it showed up together with P2495, P24C4 and P06A3.
s: Check engine light on, often with further bypass codes
Bypass position in the live data does not match the command
c: Worn or defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Deposits shifting the learned end positions
Unstable 5 V reference shared with other sensors

P2494.d: P2494 is set when the raw voltage of the bank 1 bypass position sensor drops toward zero. GM documents it for the Duramax diesel: in the 2017 tables the signal must be below 1 % of the 5 V reference in 200 of 250 samples, checked every 6.25 ms once cranking is over and the powertrain relay supplies more than 11 V.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Bypass control falls back to a default position
c: Open 5 V reference wire to the sensor
Internal sensor fault in the bypass valve

P2495.d: P2495 covers a bank 1 bypass position signal that climbs close to the reference voltage. On GM Duramax diesels the 2017 calibration fails it above 99 % of 5 V in 200 out of 250 samples, with the same enable conditions as the low test, and rates it Type B.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Additional sensor supply codes stored at the same time
c: Defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Fault in the shared 5 V reference circuit
Signal wire touching a voltage source

P2496.d: P2496 targets a bank 1 bypass position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the flap can physically move, without staying outside the electrical limits long enough for P2494 or P2495. No manufacturer documents P2496 publicly; GM's Duramax tables, which do cover the same analog sensor, only list the low, high and learning checks.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Bypass position value jumps in the live data
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking inside the insulation from engine movement
Worn contact track inside the sensor

P2497.d: P2497 is the generic circuit fault of the position sensor on the bank 2 cooler bypass, so it can only appear on engines whose second bank has its own EGR cooler with feedback-controlled flap. We found no manufacturer that documents a bank 2 bypass sensor; all published examples, such as GM's Duramax tables, are single-bank engines that use P2494 and P2495 on bank 1.
s: Check engine light on
Bypass on bank 2 no longer regulated
c: Damaged wiring to the bank 2 position sensor
Failed position sensor or bypass valve

P2498.d: With P2498 the bank 2 bypass position signal is electrically valid but not believable, for example because it does not change when the flap is commanded, settles at an unexpected value or no longer matches the end stops learned earlier. There is no public manufacturer description for this bank 2 code.
s: Check engine light on
Measured and commanded bypass position differ on bank 2
c: Worn bank 2 bypass valve with built-in sensor
Flap binding so the sensor reads a position other than commanded
End-stop learn values invalid after a repair

P2499.d: P2499 stands for a bank 2 bypass position voltage that has fallen to the bottom of its range. No manufacturer documents the bank 2 code publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 bypass position reads near zero
c: 5 V sensor supply interrupted or pulled down

P249A.d: P249A is logged when the bank 2 bypass position signal sits near the top of the reference voltage. Like its siblings on this bank, it is not described by any manufacturer in public documents.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Bank 2 bypass position shows full scale
c: Lost ground at the bank 2 position sensor
Signal wire in contact with a supply line
Water ingress in the sensor connector

P249B.d: P249B flags short dropouts or implausible jumps in the bank 2 bypass position signal that are too brief to count as a steady low or high fault. Public manufacturer documentation for it does not exist, and even the well documented bank 1 sensor on GM's Duramax only has low, high and learning checks, without an erratic test of its own.
s: Check engine light appears now and then
Bank 2 position value flickers in the live data
c: Fretting or loose terminal in the bank 2 sensor plug
Harness brittle from heat near the turbocharger

P249C.d: P249C covers the SCR dosing strategy rather than a part: after start-up the engine controller is expected to switch from fixed, map-based urea dosing to dosing corrected by the NOx sensor signal, and this code means that switch happened too seldom or too late. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks how much of the operating time was really spent in closed loop compared with what was expected, with SCR temperature between
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
NOx sensor or exhaust temperature codes may be stored as well
c: Downstream NOx sensor slow to become ready or faulty, so closed loop cannot start
Implausible exhaust gas temperature signal upstream or downstream of the SCR
Mostly short or cold trips keep the SCR below its working temperature
Engine control software calibration requiring an update

P249D.d: With P249D the NOx feedback loop of the SCR system has pushed its long-term correction as far as it may go because the delivered amount of DEF appears too small for the measured NOx. GM's tables judge this via the long-term adaptation value: above 1.69 in the 2014 diesel table and above 1.99 in the 2018 table; both rate it Type B, lamp after the second failing trip.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Increased DEF warnings or later speed or power limitation
SCR efficiency code may follow
c: Dosing valve partly blocked by urea crystals or deposits
Weak DEF pump or restricted supply line and filter
Diluted or wrong fluid in the DEF tank
NOx sensor reading too high and misleading the controller

P249E.d: P249E is the counterpart to P249D: here the SCR feedback has trimmed the dosing down to the lowest correction it is allowed, because more reductant seems to arrive than the NOx reading calls for. GM's 2014 diesel table flags a long-term adaptation factor below 0.41 (Type B); the 2018 table lists the low-side check as a two-trip Type B fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Ammonia smell from the exhaust
White crystalline deposits at the dosing point
c: Dosing valve leaking or sticking partly open
Ammonia slip from an aged or overloaded SCR catalyst seen by the NOx sensor

P249F.d: During an active filter regeneration the controller is meant to steer the temperature ahead of the particulate filter with feedback from the exhaust temperature sensors, usually by adjusting late fuel injection or a hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust. P249F is stored when the regeneration spent too little of its duration in that feedback mode.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration may take longer or repeat more often
Often no change in driveability
c: Engine or aftertreatment module software needing an update
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of the oxidation catalyst or filter reading wrongly
Hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust restricted or slow to respond
Regenerations repeatedly interrupted by short trips or changing load

P24A0.d: P24A0 means the regeneration temperature loop is already giving all the extra heat it may, yet the gas ahead of the particulate filter stays below target. GM describes it as an HC injector control deviation: the gap between setpoint and measured temperature ahead of the DPF is watched while the filter warms up, and 10 failing out of 20 samples set a Type B fault; the 2014 table phrases it as insufficient hydrocarbon
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regenerations take long or do not finish
Soot load codes may follow
c: Hydrocarbon dosing valve or its fuel supply restricted
Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the fuel does not burn ahead of the filter
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensors cooling the gas

P24A1.d: Here the regeneration loop has reduced its heat input as far as possible, but the temperature ahead of the filter still runs above target. GM lists P24A1 as the negative-deviation branch of the HC injector control check in steady regeneration, again a Type B fault counted over samples; the 2014 table calls it excessive hydrocarbon injector authority, and the 2018 table shows the check behind a calibration enable flag
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration aborted early
Possible high exhaust temperature warning
c: Hydrocarbon doser or fuel injector leaking extra fuel into the exhaust
Fuel supply part causing unstable doser pressure (Hino 2020 bubbler filter)
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
Heavy soot load burning faster than the controller can follow

P24A2.d: P24A2 judges the outcome of a regeneration on the bank 1 filter: the event ended, but the estimated soot left in the filter is still above the allowed level. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs this once per regeneration for up to 40 minutes and compares the soot estimate at the end with a threshold.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or filter warning on
More frequent regenerations, higher fuel consumption
Reduced power if soot keeps building
c: Regenerations interrupted by short trips or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature not reaching target (doser, oxidation catalyst, sensors)
Differential pressure sensor or its hoses giving a wrong soot estimate

P24A3.d: P24A3 is the bank 2 entry for a particulate filter whose soot load, estimated from differential pressure, exhaust flow and a soot model, has climbed to the point where it noticeably restricts flow and needs a regeneration. It only appears on engines with two separate filter strands, such as some V engines.
s: Particulate filter or engine warning lamp
Reduced power or slow response
Higher fuel consumption
c: Mostly short trips so passive and active regeneration cannot finish
Excess soot from injectors, EGR or boost problems
Differential pressure sensor or hoses on bank 2 giving a false high reading

P24A4.d: P24A4 marks the critical stage for the bank 1 filter: the soot load is so high that a normal regeneration risks overheating and cracking the substrate. Deutz names P24A4-00 a critical soot load.
s: Marked loss of power, limp mode
Automatic regeneration no longer runs
Malfunction indicator and filter warning lamp on
c: Earlier soot warnings or failed regenerations not dealt with
Excess soot from injectors, EGR valve or turbocharger faults
Filter saturated with ash at end of service life
Differential pressure measurement reading falsely high

P24A5.d: P24A5 means the bank 1 cooler bypass is mechanically stuck, and makers read that in both directions. GM's 2017 Duramax DC-motor flap is judged stuck in bypass if the position is still above 15 % after P245B; the 2018 vacuum version is moved between both modes and fails when the gas temperature after the cooler barely reacts, both Type B.
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up or more soot when the flap is stuck in cooling
Higher NOx and EGR gas temperatures when stuck in bypass
c: Bypass flap seized by soot and carbon deposits
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply no longer moving the flap
Incorrect EGR cooler fitted at the factory
Engine software that sets the fault too readily

P24A6.d: P24A6 is reserved for a mechanically stuck cooler bypass on bank 2. No manufacturer documents it publicly; the Ford and GM diesel summaries that describe the stuck test all apply it to a single bank and use P24A5.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven exhaust temperatures between the two banks
c: Missing vacuum on a pneumatically switched bypass

P24A7.d: Some diesel engines feed the EGR cooler with an electric auxiliary coolant pump so the cooler gets flow at low engine speed or after shut-off, independent of the main pump. P24A7 means the engine controller sees an open or otherwise faulty control line to this pump, typically when the driver stage detects no load while switching.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR may be reduced, NOx output rises
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged pump connector
Broken control wire in the harness
Open winding or electronics in the pump

P24A8.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P24A8 is about the pump's effect: it is commanded on, the wiring looks fine, yet the controller concludes that it does not deliver, for example because its speed feedback stays low or the expected temperature drop across the EGR cooler is missing. Air trapped after a coolant change, a blocked impeller, low coolant level or a seized motor are the usual reasons.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Coolant loss or bubbling at the expansion tank
EGR temperature or cooler efficiency codes may follow
c: Air pocket in the auxiliary circuit after service or a leak
Pump motor seized or impeller blocked

P24A9.d: P24A9 reports that the voltage on the control line of the electric EGR cooler coolant pump is lower than the driver stage expects in its current switching state, which usually points to a harness or pump-internal short to ground, or to a chafed wire touching the engine block. Whether low means switched on permanently or not at all depends on how the manufacturer drives the pump (low-side or high-side switching, or a
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump may run continuously or not at all
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Insulation melted near exhaust or EGR parts
Internal short in the pump electronics

P24AA.d: With P24AA the controller finds the control line of the EGR cooler coolant pump at a higher voltage than its switching state allows. The classic causes are a short circuit toward battery voltage, for example where the harness rubs against a powered wire, moisture in the connector, or a pump that no longer draws current so the line floats up.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump may not run when commanded
c: Control wire shorted to a battery voltage feed
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Pump electronics failed so no current is drawn

P24AB.d: P24AB is set when the EGR cooler coolant pump keeps running although the controller has switched it off, seen for instance in continued speed feedback or current draw. Causes include a driver stage or relay that stays closed, a short that bypasses the switching side, or pump electronics that ignore the command.
s: Pump audible after engine shut-off
Battery drained after standing
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Relay or controller output stage stuck closed
Short in the harness bypassing the switched side
Pump electronics no longer responding to the command

P24AC.d: Electronically commutated coolant pumps often report their state back to the controller on a separate feedback wire, typically as a speed or diagnostic signal. P24AC means that this return line sits below its valid range: shorted to ground, pulled down by a damaged pump, or permanently in an error level the pump uses to signal a dry run or blockage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR possibly reduced
c: Pump signalling an internal fault, dry run or blockage
Corroded feedback pin in the connector

P24AD.d: P24AD is the high-side counterpart of P24AC: the return signal from the EGR cooler coolant pump stays above its valid band. Since such feedback lines are usually pulled up inside the controller, a broken wire or a disconnected pump often shows as a constantly high level, as can a short to a voltage feed.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no noticeable effect while driving
c: Feedback wire broken or pump unplugged, line pulled high
Feedback wire shorted to a voltage feed
Pump electronics no longer pulling the signal down

P24AE.d: The resistive particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter collects soot on interlocking electrodes; a rising current between them shows that particles are leaking through the filter. P24AE covers a fault in that electrode circuit.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter efficiency monitor cannot complete
c: Sensor element contaminated or damaged by moisture
Harness or connector to the sensor control unit damaged by heat or water
Fault in the separate sensor control unit

P24AF.d: P24AF tests whether the particulate matter sensor behaves plausibly while it burns itself clean. During that heated phase the electrodes must show a small but definite current, and the heater must change the signal in an expected way.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no change in driveability
c: Sensor element aged or glazed, no longer responding
Sensor heater weak so the regeneration temperature is not reached
Element cracked by condensate after cold start

P24B0.d: P24B0 flags an electrode signal of the particulate matter sensor that sits too low, typically an open line or a cracked element that no longer conducts as expected. Ford's 2023 diesel summary watches the electrode supply continuously while the sensor measures and sets the code when it drops below 41.55 V for about 1.6 s.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Sensor element cracked or electrode interrupted
Open electrode line between sensor and sensor control unit
Sensor control unit cannot supply the electrode voltage

P24B1.d: P24B1 reports the electrode side of the particulate matter sensor reading high, which usually points to a short to a voltage source or to a soaked, conductive element. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it when electrode current exceeds 41 µA for about 3 s during measurement.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Condensate on the sensor element making it conductive
Electrode line shorted to a voltage source
Internal sensor fault, replacement sensor needed

P24B2.d: P24B2 stands for a PM sensor electrode reading that cuts out or jumps for short moments rather than staying permanently low or high. Such dropouts usually come from a loose pin, a chafed harness near the hot exhaust or moisture in the connector.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Harness chafing on hot exhaust parts
Engine control software that needs reprogramming

P24B3.d: P24B3 means the heater inside the particulate matter sensor cannot draw the current it should while it is switched on, typically because the heater line is open. The heater is needed to burn soot off the electrodes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Heater element burnt out inside the sensor
False detection in the control software

P24B4.d: P24B4 is a plausibility check on the heater of the particulate matter sensor, and makers apply it differently. Ford's 2023 diesel summary looks during measurement, with the heater switched off, and sets the code if heater voltage still exceeds 7 V for 2 s.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (not with every manufacturer)
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Protection tube of the sensor blocked by soot or deposits
Heater element aged and heating too slowly
Extra resistance in the heater harness
Heater output in the sensor control unit not switching off

P24B5.d: P24B5 points to the heater line of the particulate matter sensor being pulled toward ground, so the heater control sees an implausible current while heating is requested. GM's 18OBDG04 table describes it as a ground fault on the heater line and flags it when current is under 0.5 A or above 15 A with the heater commanded on, 30 of 60 samples, Type B with two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Internal heater fault in the sensor
False detection by the control software

P24B6.d: P24B6 reports the heater of the particulate matter sensor carrying current although it is commanded off, the classic sign of a battery-side short or a stuck driver stage in the sensor control unit. GM's 18OBDG04 table sets it when more than 0.2 A flows with the heater off or when the switch state disagrees with the command in one of the last five readings, Type B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Sensor may fail again quickly if the short is not fixed
c: Heater line shorted to battery voltage
Heater output stage in the sensor control unit stuck on
Sensor element damaged by uncontrolled heating

P24B7.d: P24B7 concerns the resistance of the heater element in the particulate matter sensor, which drifts as the platinum track ages. Ford's 2023 diesel summary measures it once per drive right after key-on, with the sensor between -30 and 150 °C, and sets the code if resistance leaves 1.06 to 2.93 Ω at the cold end or 1.81 to 4.12 Ω at the warm end.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Sensor regeneration may stay incomplete
c: Wrong sensor temperature distorting the expected value

P24B8.d: P24B8 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor that sits inside an evaporative leak check module together with the pump and the switching valve. The sensor gets a 5 V reference from the engine computer and reports canister-side pressure during the engine-off leak test.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor does not complete
c: Open or shorted 5 V reference, ground or signal wire to the leak check module
Corroded or loose connector at the leak check module near the canister
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
Engine control module does not supply the sensor reference

P24B9.d: P24B9 means the leak check module's pressure sensor delivers a signal that is electrically valid but not believable. GM's 2018 Volt table (ELCP) compares the absolute sensor reading with barometric pressure from the MAP sensor while pump and valve rest; a gap above 3,000 Pa at the engine-off wake-ups (roughly 4 to 11 h after shutdown) or above 15,000 to 20,000 Pa while driving counts as a fail, 50 of 63 samples, Type
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test aborted, readiness not set
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Pressure sensor in the leak check module drifted or noisy
Engine control software needing an update (FCA bulletins)
Moisture or dirt in the module's pressure port
Chafed wiring or loose pin causing signal disturbance

P24BA.d: P24BA reports that the voltage from the leak check module's pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest value a working sensor can produce. In GM's ELCP tables (2018 Volt) the limit is 0.70 V, about 14 % of the reference or roughly 47 kPa absolute, with 640 failures in 800 samples taken every 12.5 ms; the check runs whenever the controller is awake and is Type B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test not run
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed

P24BB.d: P24BB is stored when the leak check module's pressure signal climbs above the top of its usable range. GM uses 4.85 V, about 97 % of the reference or roughly 120 kPa, again with 640 of 800 samples and Type B; the limit appears unchanged from the 2018 Volt up to GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A for conventional ELCP systems.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test not run, readiness incomplete
c: Open sensor ground or signal wire, letting the input float high
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed

P24BC.d: P24BC is meant for a pressure signal from the leak check module that drops out or jumps briefly, too short to latch the low or high limit. No manufacturer documents P24BC publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
EVAP readiness monitor completes only occasionally
c: Loose or spread terminal in the leak check module connector
Harness chafing near the canister or tank, intermittent short or break
Water or corrosion in the module connector
Sensor in the leak check module failing intermittently

P24BD.d: P24BD points to the drive circuit of the switching valve inside the leak check module. This small solenoid moves the canister vent path between open air and the reference orifice, so the module can first measure a known leak and then test the real system.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test does not run
On some designs fuel door locked or purge disabled
c: Switching valve coil open inside the leak check module
Open control or supply wire, blown fuse or relay fault
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

P24BE.d: P24BE says the voltage on the switching valve control line is too low while the valve should be idle. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the valve sits in the ELCM leak check unit, is supplied by the MFI relay and grounded by a transistor in the engine computer, and the code sets when the line reads 3 V or less for 2 s with the valve not commanded.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open with the opener switch
Refuelling system service message on the display
c: No supply from the relay to the valve (fuse, relay, wire)
Switching valve coil open inside the module
Control wire between module and ECM shorted to ground

P24BF.d: P24BF flags too much current in the switching valve circuit while the valve is energised. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV measures coil current through its low-side driver and sets the code when it reaches 2 A or more for 2 s with the valve commanded on.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door stays locked
Canister purge switched off
c: Switching valve coil shorted inside the module
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

P24C0.d: P24C0 is a mechanical fault found during the leak test itself: the switching valve stays in its energised position, or the pump around it does not do its job. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV checks this when the parked car wakes its controller 5 h, 6 h or 8.5 h after shutdown.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open
Refuelling system service message
c: Switching valve mechanically stuck inside the leak check module
Leak detection pump stuck on or not running
Open or shorted pump circuit or connector damage
Module pressure sensor frozen at one value

P24C1.d: P24C1 means the switching valve does not respond when commanded, so the vent path stays where it was. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV recognises this after the reference measurement of the engine-off leak test: energising the valve should change the canister pressure, and if the difference to the first or second reference value stays below a limit for 10 s, the code is stored.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open
EVAP readiness not set
c: Switching valve stuck in rest position inside the module
Open or shorted valve circuit so the valve never moves
Dirt or water from the vent line jamming the valve seat

P24C2.d: Diesel exhaust lines often carry three or four temperature probes in a row, ahead of the oxidation catalyst, the particulate filter and the SCR catalyst. P24C2 says that on bank 1 the readings of these probes no longer agree with each other, without pinning the error on one of them.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration suppressed or aborted
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: One exhaust temperature probe has drifted with age and reads too high or too low
Corroded or heat-damaged connector adding resistance to one probe signal
Engine control software with too tight correlation limits (update available on some models)
Probes swapped between mounting positions after a repair

P24C3.d: P24C3 is the bank 2 counterpart of P24C2 and only makes sense on engines whose two cylinder banks feed separate exhaust strings, each with its own set of temperature probes. The controller has found that the probes of the second string disagree among themselves beyond what the operating state allows.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration may be inhibited
c: One bank 2 temperature probe has drifted and no longer matches the others
Contact resistance in a bank 2 probe connector or harness
Exhaust leak near one probe cooling its tip

P24C4.d: The bypass flap of the EGR cooler learns its end stops, and P24C4 means the learned values for bank 1 have left the window the software accepts. GM's diesel tables from 2017 on run the learning after key-off with coolant between 70 and 129 °C: the raw signal must lie between 16 and 24 % of 5 V in cooling position and between 72 and 85 % in bypass position; outside, the code is stored as Type B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after the second trip
Reduced EGR cooling, higher NOx output
Often no change in driveability
c: Worn bypass valve whose integrated position sensor no longer reaches its learned values
Soot deposits shifting the end stops of the flap
Signal offset from connector corrosion or a weak 5 V reference
Learning repeatedly cut short because the controller is woken right after key-off

P24C5.d: P24C5 belongs to engines with a second EGR cooler and bypass flap on bank 2. It reports that the end positions learned by that flap's position sensor fall outside the accepted window, so the controller can no longer trust where the flap really stands.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher NOx emissions due to poorly controlled EGR cooling
c: Worn bank 2 bypass valve or sensor track
Deposits changing the end positions of the bank 2 flap
Signal shift caused by wiring or connector resistance

P24C6.d: Inside the particulate matter sensor a meander-shaped platinum track measures element temperature, which the sensor needs to control its heater. P24C6 is the general circuit fault of that temperature signal.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Open or shorted temperature line in the harness
Fault in the sensor control unit

P24C7.d: P24C7 checks whether the temperature the particulate matter sensor reports fits the exhaust around it. Ford's 2023 diesel summary does an offset test after a cold soak of at least 6 hours, flagging more than 45 °C against the mean of the exhaust temperature sensors, and a dynamic test while driving that fails below -150 or above 60 °C against a model.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Sensor element damaged or temperature track drifted
Extra resistance between sensor and sensor control unit
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor used as reference

P24C8.d: P24C8 would be set when the temperature signal of the particulate matter sensor sits below its valid range, for example because the meander line is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the available summaries fold low and high readings into other codes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Internal fault of the sensor element

P24C9.d: P24C9 reports the PM sensor temperature reading stuck at the high end, which GM explains as a short toward supply voltage or a broken meander line. In GM's 25OBDG04A diesel table the sensor control unit checks the meander signal and its reference: a signal under 0.3 V or over 3.5 V, or a reference under 4.5 V, counts as a failure, and 24 failures in a row or 24 of 96 samples set a Type B code with two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Broken temperature lead near the sensor body
Temperature line shorted to a voltage source
Reference voltage of the temperature circuit too low

P24CA.d: P24CA is reserved for a PM sensor temperature reading that fails only now and then instead of staying out of range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp coming and going
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Cracked joint inside the sensor lead

P24CB.d: Some SCR diesels have a switch at the DEF filler neck that tells the engine controller when the cap is opened, so a refill can be recognised and the tank level and fluid quality reassessed. P24CB is the general circuit code for this switch: the controller sees a signal that fits neither the open nor the closed state.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often right after refilling DEF
Refill not recognised, DEF warnings may persist
c: Cap microswitch sticking, especially in hot and humid conditions
Corroded connector or chafed wire at the filler neck
Dried DEF crystals around the switch actuator

P24CC.d: P24CC is a plausibility fault: the cap switch at the DEF filler neck delivers an electrically valid signal, but its behaviour does not match what else the controller knows, for instance a switch that still reports an open cap long after refilling, or one that never changes state while the tank level clearly rose. Audi names the code in bulletin 2051053 (and its revision) for the 2013 to 2015 Q7 TDI, where the AdBlue
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after a DEF refill
Fill level or refill message not updated
c: Switch stuck in one position so it no longer follows the cap
DEF residue hindering the switch plunger
Damaged or non-original filler cap that does not actuate the switch

P24CD.d: P24CD means the signal line of the DEF cap switch sits below its valid voltage band. With the usual pull-up input that points to the line being pulled to ground: a short in the harness near the filler neck, a switch with an internal short, or moisture bridging the contacts.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cap state shown permanently wrong, refills not detected
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground near the filler neck
Moisture or DEF in the switch or connector bridging to ground

P24CE.d: With P24CE the controller sees the DEF cap switch signal above its permitted band. On a pull-up input this typically happens when the line is open, because the input then floats up to the reference, or when it touches a supply wire; a broken switch contact can look the same.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Refill of DEF not registered
c: Disconnected plug or broken wire letting the input float high
Signal wire touching a supply line

P24CF.d: P24CF is stored when the DEF cap switch signal jumps between states or drops out briefly although nobody touches the cap, typically while driving over rough roads. The controller counts unexpected changes and flags the circuit as unstable even if every single value lies within limits.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, sometimes coming and going
Spurious refill or cap-open messages
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the switch connector
Switch that sticks only partly and chatters
Harness rubbing on the tank or body

P24D0.d: P24D0 concerns the power feed of the particulate matter sensor and its control unit, which sinks when the supply line has excess resistance or a short toward ground. Ford's 2023 diesel summary compares battery voltage with the voltage at the sensor while the heater runs at 35 % duty or more, and sets the code if the drop exceeds 1.1 V, 2.1 V or 3 V depending on battery level, within 2 s.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Further particulate sensor codes stored at the same time
c: Corroded fuse, relay contact or ground adding resistance
Fault in the sensor control unit

P24D1.d: Before each measurement the particulate matter sensor heats its element to burn off collected soot. P24D1 means that this cleaning phase did not finish properly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Sensor heater degraded, not reaching cleaning temperature
Heavy deposits on the sensor element

P24D2.d: Besides the control output, many DEF heaters have a sense line on which the controller reads back the voltage actually reaching the element. P24D2 marks a general fault on this sense circuit for heater A, such as an open lead or a reading that makes no sense at all, as opposed to the voltage being merely too low (P248A) or too high (P248B).
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF warnings in cold weather, dosing delayed after a cold start
c: Broken or disconnected sense wire to heater A
DEF creep or water corroding the heater connector
Faulty measuring input in the SCR or engine control module

P24D3.d: P24D3 is the same kind of fault for heater B, which GM and Ford assign to the heated DEF line from pump to dosing valve. The read-back line of this heater is broken or delivers nonsense, so the controller cannot tell whether the hose is really powered; the narrower low and high cases are P248C and P248D.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF dosing faults or warnings at low temperatures
c: Open sense wire or loose plug at the heated DEF line
Damaged heated line with internal conductor fault
Manufacturer-specific use of the code (FCA uses it for PM sensor supply), software update

P24D4.d: Where an electric auxiliary pump moves coolant through the EGR cooler, the pump usually reports back to the engine controller on a separate wire, for example with a speed or status signal. P24D4 is the general fault of that feedback circuit: the signal is missing or cannot be interpreted, while the narrower cases of a line stuck below or above its band are P24AC and P24AD.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR reduced, possibly higher NOx and changed engine noise
Coolant temperature warnings if the pump really stops
c: Open feedback wire or loose connector at the pump
Failed pump electronics no longer sending a status signal
Blown fuse or failed relay leaving the pump without power

P24D5.d: P24D5 is the general circuit code for a second EVAP pressure sensor, called B to tell it apart from the main sensor A (P0450 range). Which sensor is B depends on the maker: Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV uses it for an absolute fuel tank pressure sensor on its sealed tank, GM for a canister vapour pressure sensor, and Audi's bulletin 2069531 assigns sensor 2 to the G950 part in the purge path.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor incomplete
c: Open or shorted reference, ground or signal wire of sensor B
Loose or corroded connector at sensor B

P24D6.d: P24D6 is a plausibility fault of EVAP pressure sensor B. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A checks the canister vapour pressure sensor at the start of a cold drive: after more than 3,600 s soak the offset must sit within a window around barometric pressure; a filtered ratio above 0.73 sets the code, Type A.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Other EVAP codes such as a switching valve fault may appear alongside
No driveability change
c: Wrong sensor version installed (GM HD trucks, narrow-range instead of wide-range)
Sensor offset drifted away from barometric pressure
Kinked hose or blocked port at the sensor
Engine control software needing an update (FCA, Audi)

P24D7.d: P24D7 is set when EVAP pressure sensor B sends a voltage below its valid window. GM's 2023 table (23OBDG03A) watches its canister pressure sensor continuously and fails below 0.15 V, 3 % of the reference, with 640 of 800 samples, Type B; the sensor normally works between 0.5 and 4.5 V.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP tests suspended
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground

P24D8.d: P24D8 reports EVAP pressure sensor B reading above its valid voltage. In GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A the canister pressure sensor fails above 4.85 V, 97 % of the reference, counted over 640 of 800 samples and treated as Type B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor incomplete
c: Open ground of sensor B, signal floats high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage

P24D9.d: P24D9 covers a sensor B signal that keeps flickering instead of failing outright. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV runs this check once per drive cycle inside the parked leak test, when the controller wakes at its scheduled times and coolant and intake air lie between 4 and 35 °C.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Refuelling system service message on the display
c: Loose terminal or poor contact at the tank pressure sensor
Harness chafed along the fuel tank
Tank pressure or tank differential pressure sensor unstable

P24DA.d: P24DA checks that the particulate matter sensor actually samples exhaust gas, which is how the system detects a sensor that has been pulled out, sits in a blocked protection tube or is mounted wrongly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs it once per drive in protective heating mode and fails it if the summed sensor voltage change during exhaust flow changes stays under 0.5 V, over about 3 minutes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
c: Sensor removed from the exhaust or installed wrongly
Sensor no longer responding to exhaust flow

P24DB.d: After shut-down an SCR system empties its lines back into the tank so no fluid freezes in them; in Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 a 4/2-way valve in the supply module reverses the flow for this. Valve B is a second purge valve, for instance in layouts with two dosing branches.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line not purged after shut-off, freezing risk in winter
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector to purge valve B
Open solenoid winding in valve B
DEF-induced corrosion in the supply module connector

P24DC.d: P24DC judges purge valve B by its effect, not by its wiring: once the controller switches the valve to purge, the pressure in the DEF line it serves should fall noticeably, and here it did not. No manufacturer documents P24DC publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Frozen DEF line or dosing fault after cold nights
c: Valve B mechanically stuck by crystallised DEF
Blocked return path or filter in the supply module

P24DD.d: P24DD means the control line of purge valve B shows too little voltage at a moment when it should be high. With the low-side switching that GM uses for valve A, this is checked while the driver is off: the line should then carry battery voltage through the coil, and a low reading indicates a short to ground between valve and controller, so the valve may sit energised permanently.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Valve may remain in purge position, dosing pressure not reached
c: Control wire chafed to ground near tank or frame
Valve coil shorted to its housing
Water or DEF in the connector

P24DE.d: With P24DE the control line of purge valve B stays at high voltage while the controller is actually pulling it to ground to switch the valve. That points to a short to the battery feed on the wire between valve and controller, or a valve coil with too little resistance, so that the driver protects itself and the valve never shifts.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line not purged, frozen line after frost
c: Control wire touching a supply line
Valve coil with shorted turns and too low resistance
Damaged driver stage in the control module

P24DF.d: Stuck open means purge valve B remains in, or leaks toward, its emptying position while the system should be dosing. Part of the pump flow then goes back to the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, drops quickly when the pump stops, or needs a high pump duty to hold.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF pressure too low, reduced dosing and rising NOx
Warnings about reduced SCR function, possibly later engine power limits
c: Internal leak or worn seat in purge valve B
DEF crystals preventing the valve from returning to dosing position
Control circuit fault keeping the valve energised

P24E0.d: Stuck closed means purge valve B does not move into its emptying position when commanded after shut-down, so the line it serves stays filled with fluid under residual pressure. In normal dosing this goes unnoticed; the risk appears in frost, when the trapped DEF freezes in hose, pump or injector and can crack them.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Frozen or burst DEF line or injector after frost
c: Valve B seized by crystallised DEF or corrosion
Weak coil that no longer pulls the valve over
Intermittent open in the control circuit during shut-down

P24E1.d: An NH3 sensor behind the SCR catalyst measures ammonia that slipped through unused, letting the controller trim dosing and detect overdosing or an aged catalyst. P24E1 is the general circuit code for this sensor: its signal is missing, implausible or erratic.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Less precise DEF dosing, possible ammonia smell or higher NOx
c: NH3 sensor element or its electronics failed from heat and age
Heat-damaged wiring or connector near the exhaust
Software calibration issue, update available on some engines

P24E2.d: P24E2 flags an NH3 sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense: the ammonia value sticks, drifts or contradicts what the dosing model expects from the SCR catalyst. On heavy trucks the sensor is a smart unit with its own electronics that test probe and circuitry and report over J1939.
s: Check engine light after two trips
DEF consumption noticeably higher or lower than usual
Possible ammonia smell at the tailpipe
c: Sensing element aged or poisoned by deposits, giving a drifting ammonia value
Urea crystals around the sensor tip after overdosing
Exhaust leak near the sensor diluting the sample

P24E3.d: P24E3 means the NH3 sensor signal lies below the lowest value an intact sensor can deliver. Usual culprits are a short to ground between probe and its electronics module, a terminal pushed back in the connector or a defect inside the probe.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Scan tool shows ammonia reading stuck at minimum
c: Chafed harness between probe and sensor module shorting to ground
Internal fault in the ammonia probe
Corroded or pushed-back terminal at the probe connector

P24E4.d: P24E4 is set when the NH3 sensor signal climbs above anything a working sensor could report, so the value is rejected as electrically impossible rather than merely implausible. Typical reasons are a short to a supply voltage, a broken line pulled up internally, or failing electronics that output a saturated value.
s: Check engine light on
Ammonia reading pinned at the upper limit
Possible reduced DEF dosing
c: Signal line shorted to a supply voltage in the harness
Open line between probe and module read as maximum value
Sensor electronics module outputting a saturated value

P24E5.d: P24E5 covers an NH3 sensor signal that jumps or drops out for short moments while staying mostly in range. Vibration, heat cycling of the exhaust and road salt make loose connector pins and cracked insulation near the SCR can the main suspects.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Live data shows spikes in the ammonia value
c: Loose or corroded pins at the sensor or module connector
Harness insulation cracked by exhaust heat and vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor electronics

P24E6.d: Like a NOx sensor, the ammonia sensor only measures once its ceramic element is hot, so it carries an electric heater. P24E6 reports that this heater circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty: the driver commands heating but sees no current flowing.
s: Check engine light on
No ammonia reading after warm-up
c: Heater element inside the NH3 probe burnt through
Broken wire in the sensor pigtail near the hot exhaust
Heater terminal without contact in the connector

P24E7.d: P24E7 points to a heater circuit of the NH3 sensor that reads too low: the feedback voltage stays near ground, or the current is far below what the heater should draw. Most often the heater feed is shorted to ground, which can also blow the fuse or switch off the driver to protect it; a heater whose resistance has risen sharply gives a similar picture.
s: Check engine light on
Ammonia value missing or delayed after start
c: Heater supply line shorted to ground
Heater element with strongly increased resistance
Blown fuse in the heater supply

P24E8.d: With P24E8 the heater circuit of the NH3 sensor reads too high. Either the line is shorted to a supply voltage so that the heater cannot be switched off, or the driver measures overcurrent because the element has failed with low resistance.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Ammonia sensor reading switched off
c: Heater control line shorted to battery voltage
Heater element failed with low resistance, causing overcurrent
Heater driver in the sensor module defective

P24E9.d: P24E9 is not about a broken wire but about how the heater works: the circuit is intact, yet the NH3 probe does not reach or hold its operating temperature in the expected time, or its temperature control swings. Deutz lists P24E9 for its MD1 engine controller as SPN 4382 with FMI 2, meaning erratic or incorrect heater data.
s: Check engine light, often together with an NH3 sensor performance code
Ammonia reading available late or unstable
c: Aged heater element no longer delivering full power
Condensate on the ceramic cooling it or causing thermal shock
Low supply voltage limiting heater power

P24EA.d: The NH3 sensor is a smart unit: its electronics module needs its own power feed, usually switched battery voltage through a fuse or relay, to run the probe, the heater and the J1939 link. P24EA is the general fault of that supply, set when the measured feed voltage is missing, unstable or otherwise outside the valid window without being classed as clearly low or high.
s: Check engine light on
Further NH3 sensor or communication codes stored
c: Fuse or relay in the sensor feed faulty or loose
Damaged or corroded power or ground wire to the sensor module
Supply monitoring in the sensor module defective

P24EB.d: P24EB reports that the power feed of the NH3 sensor module sags below its lower limit. Below that point the heater cannot bring the probe up to temperature and the electronics may reset, so ammonia readings and sensor messages become unreliable.
s: Warning lamp, often after cold starts
NH3 sensor drops off the data link at times
c: Weak or discharged batteries pulling system voltage down
High resistance in the ground path of the sensor module
Corroded fuse or relay contacts causing voltage drop

P24EC.d: P24EC is stored when the feed voltage measured at the NH3 sensor module exceeds its upper limit. Overvoltage can damage the heater driver and the electronics, so the module may switch off heating and measurement to protect itself.
s: Check engine light on
Other modules may also report high system voltage
c: Overvoltage from jump-starting or a booster charger
Sensor supply line shorted to another higher feed

P24ED.d: Every NH3 sensor leaves the factory with individual correction values for offset and gain stored in its own electronics. P24ED means this memory fails its integrity check, for instance a checksum mismatch or unreadable data, so the module cannot convert the raw probe signal into a trustworthy ammonia value.
s: Check engine light on
No valid ammonia value although wiring tests pass
c: Calibration data in the sensor module corrupted
Power loss while the module was writing data

P24EE.d: P24EE says the microcontroller inside the NH3 sensor module has failed its own self-test, for example a watchdog reset, a RAM or ROM error or a timing fault. The engine controller only learns this through the status the sensor sends, because the processor is what runs the probe, the heater and the J1939 messages.
s: Check engine light on
NH3 sensor data missing or frozen
c: Electronics of the NH3 sensor module failed
Unstable supply voltage causing processor resets
Module damaged by heat or water ingress

P24EF.d: Some control modules drive a discrete wake-up output that switches other units on before or alongside the network. P24EF reports an open circuit on that line.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Connected module stays asleep, with related communication codes
c: Broken wake-up wire in the harness
Pin pushed back or corroded in a module connector
Wake-up output of the control module defective

P24F0.d: P24F0 means that a control module drives its wake-up output on, but the line voltage stays down, pointing to a ground short or a load drawing far too much current. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module runs this check whenever the output is commanded on and reports a fault if the control voltage is at or below 5.52 V.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hybrid or charging functions unavailable
c: Wake-up line shorted to ground at a chafe point
Moisture in a connector bridging the line to ground
Receiving module loading the wake-up input too heavily

P24F1.d: With P24F1 the wake-up line carries voltage while its driving module has the output switched off, so a short to a battery feed or a second source keeps it live. GM's HPC2 module in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables flags 13.21 V or more in the off state, using the same 480-of-560 sample count at 12.5 ms and Type A, MIL after one trip.
s: Check engine light and several warning messages
Temporary no-start condition
Possible battery drain while parked
c: Wake-up line shorted to a battery feed
Signal timing between ignition module and receiving unit, solved by coding
Voltage fed back from another module that stays awake

P24F2.d: P24F2 compares two readings in the intake path of a diesel with cooled exhaust gas recirculation: the gas temperature after the EGR cooler and the air temperature behind the charge air cooler. When conditions say both should be close, for instance after the engine has cooled down, a wide gap shows that one of the two sensors cannot be trusted.
s: Check engine light, often without any noticeable driving fault
EGR operation reduced as a precaution on some calibrations
Implausible EGR or charge air temperatures in live data after a cold soak
c: Outdated PCM calibration flagging the correlation without a real fault (Chrysler 3.0 L diesel)
EGR temperature sensor drifting or sooted up
Charge air cooler outlet temperature sensor reading wrong
Corroded connector adding resistance to one sensor signal

P24F3.d: P24F3 sets the temperature reported from the DEF (reductant) tank against the fuel temperature. After a long soak both liquids rest close to ambient, so a clear mismatch exposes a sensor that reads wrong although each signal may be electrically valid.
s: Warning lamp, often after a cold start
DEF tank and fuel temperature far apart in live data after an overnight stop
c: DEF tank temperature sensor (often integrated in the tank or sender module) reading wrong
Local heat source such as an exhaust leak warming one sensor
Contact resistance in a sensor connector

P24F4.d: P24F4 concerns the dead time of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 when engine-out NOx falls, typically on lift-off into overrun: the reading stays put too long before it starts dropping, even if the later descent is normal. CARB defines this split for exhaust sensors, delayed response being the wait before the first reaction and slow response a sluggish transition.
s: Check engine light on
Front NOx value lingers on lift-off
Engine runs normally
c: Soot or oil ash on the diffusion barrier of the front sensor
Aged measuring cells reacting late to falling NOx
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the transient

P24F5.d: P24F5 is the same delay check for NOx sensor 2 on bank 1, which sits behind the SCR catalyst and judges its conversion. If its value lags when NOx at the outlet falls, the efficiency estimate is distorted and the SCR monitor could pass or fail wrongly, so the sensor must react in time.
s: Check engine light on
Possibly an SCR efficiency code alongside
c: DEF crystals or ammonia slip attacking the rear sensor element
Aged measuring cells of sensor 2 reacting late
Condensate in the cold tailpipe area affecting the sensor

P24F6.d: Heavy Volvo and Mack trucks regenerate the particulate filter with an aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector (AHI, the 7th injector) that sprays diesel ahead of the oxidation catalyst; compressed air from the truck supply then blows the line to the nozzle clear. P24F6 means the fuel/air purge valve in the AHI module seems to stay open, so air keeps flowing when it should not.
s: Particulate filter regeneration does not complete
Warning lamp and aftertreatment message on the dash
Rising soot load and more frequent regeneration requests
c: Oil or water in the purge air from an unsuitable or worn air-dryer cartridge
Debris holding the purge valve in the AHI module open
Damaged AHI nozzle or leaking fuel/air line toward the nozzle
Doser air supply pressure outside the 221 kPa specification

P24F7.d: P24F7 is the reverse case of P24F6: the purge valve of the aftertreatment fuel/air system will not open when commanded, so no compressed air reaches the dosing line and the 7th injector after a dosing phase. In Volvo and Mack trucks this valve sits in the AHI dosing block, mounted on the fuel filter housing from model year 2017 and on the engine block side before.
s: Active regeneration aborted or not started
Warning lamp with aftertreatment message
Possible engine derate as soot load climbs
c: Purge valve jammed by oil, water or particles from the air system
Air supply to the AHI module restricted or below specification
Coked or kinked line between AHI module and nozzle
Internal fault of the AHI dosing module

P24F8.d: P24F8 is the electrical fault of the fuel/air purge valve: the control unit finds the solenoid drive circuit not working, typically an open wire or a coil that draws no current. Volvo and Mack report it as P24F813, the suffix 13 meaning open circuit.
s: Warning lamp right after the circuit test runs
Active regeneration blocked or incomplete
c: Broken wire or chafed harness between engine controller and AHI module
Corroded or loose plug at the AHI dosing module
Interrupted coil of the purge valve solenoid

P24F9.d: P24F9 covers a purge valve control circuit that is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example when measured current or a feedback signal does not follow the commanded state within the expected time. Unlike P24F8, P24FA and P24FB, this variant appears in none of the Volvo/Mack AHI documents, and no manufacturer documents P24F9 publicly.
s: Warning lamp, sometimes only under heat
Irregular or aborted filter regenerations
c: Purge valve moving slowly because of deposits
Solenoid coil resistance drifting with heat or age
High-resistance contact in the module plug

P24FA.d: P24FA reports that voltage on the purge valve control line is lower than the driver stage expects in the current switching state: a short to ground on the wire, a coil with too little resistance or a weak supply. Volvo and Mack name P24FA00 in the electrical section of their AHI troubleshooting guide for US10+OBD13 and newer engines; the work there is on the dosing module plug and the harness, not on the air or fuel
s: Warning lamp shortly after key-on or during dosing
Regeneration not possible
c: Control wire chafed through to chassis ground
Purge valve coil with shorted turns
Moisture in the AHI module connector

P24FB.d: With P24FB the purge valve control line sits higher than allowed, a pattern that points to a short to battery voltage or to a broken low-side path, so the controller cannot pull the line down. In the Volvo/Mack AHI guide P24FB00 is listed right beside P24FA00 among the electrical codes, and the first check is the harness and the plug at the dosing module.
s: Warning lamp and aftertreatment message
Filter regeneration unavailable
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed in the harness
Interrupted return path between valve and controller
Controller output stage protecting itself against overcurrent

P24FC.d: P24FC concerns the output stage that powers the heater of the particulate matter sensor: the driver reports excessive current or an internal temperature past its limit, which suggests a heater with shorted turns or too little resistance, or an overheating sensor electronics unit. On heavy trucks this sensor works as a self-diagnosing device after the SCR catalyst and reports over J1939.
s: Warning lamp
No soot reading from the PM sensor, DPF monitoring not completed
c: Internal failure of the smart PM sensor (heater or electronics)
Water ingress cracking the ceramic element or shorting the heater
Unusually high exhaust temperature at the sensor, e.g. during repeated regenerations

P24FD.d: P24FD is intended to flag that the particulate filter in position A is not the expected part or is absent, for example after a filter delete or when an unsuitable replacement has been fitted. No manufacturer documents P24FD publicly.
s: Check engine light
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is missing
Emissions inspection failed
c: Particulate filter removed or replaced by a straight pipe
Leaking or blocked pressure lines making a present filter look absent

P24FE.d: P24FE means the controller concludes that the SCR catalyst is missing or not the expected part. Ford runs this test on the 6.7 L diesel (2023 summary) for about 60 s with SCR inlet at 195–340 °C and feedgas NOx of 70–500 ppm, and sets the code when cumulative SCR efficiency falls below 0 %.
s: Warning or service lamp (Hino sets the service lamp, MIL stays off)
Reduced engine power
NOx downstream of the SCR as high as upstream in live data
c: SCR catalyst removed or replaced by a non-matching part
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor misreading (Ford sensor 11, Hino NOx sensors)
Controller software detecting removal falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Diluted DEF or faulty DEF injector collapsing NOx conversion

P24FF.d: P24FF signals that the diesel exhaust fluid itself has become too hot while the engine runs. The controller reads the DEF temperature sensor in the tank and flags a value above its limit during operation; hot urea solution ages faster and can form deposits.
s: Warning lamp with SCR or DEF message
DEF tank temperature far above ambient in live data
c: DEF tank coolant solenoid valve installed against its flow direction (Volvo)
Tank heating valve stuck open so hot coolant keeps flowing
Missing heat shield or exhaust leak warming the tank or lines
DEF temperature sensor reading too high
